[89] Publications Centre for Peace Studies FOREWORD The 2002 White Paper was born from the Government's desire to take stock of the situation of the Armed Forces and, more generally, of the entire Defence sector in light of the new geopolitical framework that emerged after the mass murders perpetrated on 11 September against the United States of America

[90] Sixteen years separate us from the previous White Paper, produced in 1985 by the then Minister Spadolini

[91] In those years, the East-West confrontation was alive, with the question of the Euromissiles, but new commitments were already emerging, anticipated by the missions in Lebanon from 1982 to 1984, almost as if to announce that season of radical changes in the international scenario that would then begin in 1989, with the fall of the Berlin Wall

[92] The end of the Cold War and the disintegration of the USSR sparked ethnic, nationalist, religious, and economic tensions along the "arc of crises," as strategic experts call the vast area of the planet that begins in North Africa in the West, crosses the Middle East and the Caucasus, and extends eastward to the Gulf, Central Asia, Kashmir, and finally reaches Southeast Asia, where ethnic-religious conflicts are prevalent (think of the case of East Timor, for example

[93] To the north, this “arc of crises” extends to the Balkans, adjacent to our land and sea borders, through which a complex conflict, with ancient historical roots, has penetrated the very heart of Europe

[94] The attacks of September 11 definitively marked the new reality of global security and confirmed that the threats we will face in the future are very different in nature from those we have fought and defeated in the past, thanks to the Atlantic cohesion that has united European and North American democracies in a common effort to defend freedom

[95] Today, an identical cohesion – possibly with a broader participation of states – must counter the dark threat of terrorism, which could come to possess weapons of mass destruction and demonstrates the capacity for global organization, penetration, and proselytism not only in crisis-affected areas but even in Western societies

[96] At the same time, the other novelty that marks a radical break with the context in which the previous White Paper was developed is the different public approach to the issue of national security

[97] The large majorities recorded in Parliament in support of the missions in Albania and Kosovo, in the previous legislature, and in support of our participation in "Enduring Freedom" demonstrate that Italy has developed a full national awareness of its international responsibilities, regardless of contingent roles as majority and opposition

[98] The issues of military security, geopolitics, and geoeconomics have become topics of collective interest in Italy, too, taking on a media relevance unimaginable until recently

[99] The White Paper also intends to represent this new awareness of the problems

[100] Italy and the Italians have closely followed our soldiers in the many operations outside national borders from Africa to the Balkans to Timor

[101] They appreciated his work, his dedication to duty, his professionalism

[102] At the same time, public opinion has been an active spectator of the evolution of the military instrument, in particular the entry of women and the launch of the professional model

[103] real and incisive changes in national customs and traditions

[104] The White Paper not only serves to remind the country of the centrality of Defense, broadening and consolidating attention and consensus around the Armed Forces and their needs, but also to take a snapshot of the current situation in order to assess the effects of the process of change on the national military, compared to the military instruments of other countries around the world, within the framework of an Atlantic Alliance that is rethinking itself and a Europe striving to equip itself with a political structure also in the military field

[105] The Atlantic Alliance, after having confirmed its role in managing crises in the Balkans, has become a mechanism also characterized by an "inclusive" logic, no longer simply one of opposition to the threat

[106] The openings to the Russian Federation, following Moscow's decisive stance against international terrorism, certainly mark the end of an era and give the Alliance greater flexibility, serving both its political and military roles, within the framework of common values that unite the most recently democratic countries with those that have already consolidated it

[107] The advancement of the EU's common security and defense policy is another cornerstone of Italy's security and—more generally—of Europe and the entire planet

[108] Italy is participating in the efforts to create a first, large nucleus of European forces, as decided in Helsinki

[109] We know that the difficulties are not few, as the long, ten-year journey towards the single currency testifies

[110] However, we must continue along the path of a common security and defense policy, in parallel with the reform of the Union's institutions, which is now unavoidable, especially in light of the Union's upcoming enlargement to the East and towards the Baltic and Mediterranean regions

[111] The national Armed Forces have also changed profoundly compared to the configuration they had at the time of the previous White Paper, in

[112] The reform of the top leadership is a reality with all its beneficial consequences in terms of unity of command and joint vision of the entire military instrument

[113] i Publications Center for Peace Studies www.studiperlapace.it ____________ Carabinieri have become the fourth Armed Force

[114] The technical-operational area is still being simplified and streamlined, just like the technical-administrative and technical-industrial areas

[115] The objective of quality is pursued with greater determination even if many expectations of modernization and professionalization have been frustrated by the limited resources available

[116] a true “sword of Damocles” for national defense and whose negative effect on national security is only now being clearly and widely perceived under the pressure of the terrible threat of international terrorism

[117] In concrete terms, the legacy of the 2nd Berlusconi Government essentially consists of the large participation in peacekeeping operations, excellently carried out by our military, which however, in terms of presence, alternation and turnover, amounts to 9,000 men multiplied by

[118] that is, 27,000 soldiers or, at most

[119] A small number compared to the 112,000 men of the Army and the approximately 200,000 soldiers of the three "traditional" Armed Forces (excluding the Carabinieri, equal to another 116,000 units), at the end of the professionalization phase

[120] The numerous legislative measures passed by the governments of the past 13th legislature, despite the commendable intention of modernizing the defense tool, can be seen as a shock dose inoculated into a body that is not in perfect health because it has been malnourished for a long time or treated with the bare minimum

[121] However, this sudden and massive intervention does not yet seem capable of addressing operational needs that today are approaching the maximum capabilities of our military instrument and, moreover, in a phase of transition from compulsory conscription to voluntary service and with increasingly pressing international obligations due to the development of Islamic fundamentalist terrorist activity

[122] It is true that today Armies are no longer evaluated in quantitative terms, much less as sums of men

[123] But the relationship between Operational Departments and General Staffs is symptomatic, from which certain imbalances in presence emerge, predominantly between the Top Commands, Intermediate Commands and Educational Institutions, compared to the "operational" ones

[124] Nor does this disharmony diminish when moving to the Navy and the Air Force, where the function of the machine prevails over that of man, yet the intermediate Command structures are not perfectly sized to the complex of Ships and Flight Departments

[125] Imbalances in the use of personnel, overall undercapitalization of forces, qualitative level of the military instrument lower than the average of our main allies

[126] These appear to be the main handicaps of our Defense which can weigh, and not a little, also on Italy's role and authority in international forums

[127] Answers are needed

[128] First, the entire personnel sector requires balancing, and this will be the primary objective of the new Government, which has also set itself the goal of shortening the transition from conscription to military professionalism so as to complete the formation of a fully professionalized Armed Forces of 190,000 personnel by 2004, before the end of the current legislative session. This structural reform will naturally also extend to the entire senior management structure, which, despite the reforms implemented, comprises five General Staffs, ten Directorates General, and two Central Offices, in addition to Intermediate Commands, Inspectorates, and various entities

[129] Secondly, another area to consider is that of means and materials, where it appears necessary to define priorities more carefully

[130] On the other hand, the sector can no longer be conceived as an expression of national productivity, but as the fruit of international collaboration and cooperation, both due to the high costs incurred by new weapons systems and the need for so-called "interoperability" within the framework of our alliances

[131] The Air Force and the Navy are currently the Armed Forces suffering the most

[132] especially the Air Force, which is not only assessed in terms of aircraft, but also in terms of electronic control of airspace

[133] The recent terrorist attack on the United States has dramatically highlighted the urgent need to ensure security from attacks from the air

[134] Unfortunately, Italy's shortcomings in this sector are very significant and are exaggerated by the lack of manned interceptors, missiles, and radar

[135] Therefore, airspace control, which is part of the primary task of the Armed Forces in the context of territorial defense, in its fullest sense of defense of the State, in Article 1 of Law No. 331 on the suspension of compulsory military service, will constitute an urgent priority for the near future

[136] The Navy is not experiencing better times, also because the prolonged use of the vessels in naval blockade duties and interventions carried out in the last decade has excessively worn out the ships, shortening their average lifespan calculated on the basis of the employment rates of the Cold War era

[137] Finally, attention must inevitably focus on the Defense budget, which cannot be separated from the Defense model

[138] The 2002 Defense budget set by the previous Government amounted to 36,837 billion, equal to 1.48% of GDP

[139] But the share allocated to the “defense function” is 26,460 billion, equal to 1.06% of GDP

[140] If we compare these data with similar data from other NATO countries, we find some negative differences

[141] In fact, France allocates 1.75% to the defense function, England 2.48%, Germany 1.18%, but with a GDP 70% higher than Italy's. A deeper analysis of the resources that Italy allocates to the "defense function" reveals that approximately half of the resources (48%) are allocated to personnel, 26% to operating expenses and 26% to investments

[142] It is true that, compared to the 2001 budget, there has been an increase of 8.2%, but it is also true that the breakdown of expenses for personnel, operations, and investment shows a much higher increase for personnel (+11.6%) than for operations (+3.0%) and investment (+8.0%

[143] The reasons given to justify these differences are all based on the transition from "leverage" to "professionalism" which inevitably causes an increase in costs in this sector

[144] However, it is undeniable that we are faced with an "unbalanced budget" and the ideal division of 2/3 to personnel and operations and 1/3 to investments is still a distant goal

[145] The rational solution to Italy's defense problem can only come from the adoption of a well-defined defense model based on actual budget availability

[146] It will therefore be necessary to review the current architecture of the Armed Forces in all its military and civilian components, eliminating all those intermediate structures between the top and the base in favor of the operational forces, also reducing the transition times between "conscription" and "professionalism

[147] We must eliminate everything that does not comply with the fulfillment of the obligations that come from our main alliances

[148] NATO, the EU and the UN, establishing priorities to be met with specific budget items

[149] In conclusion, with this White Paper, the Ministry of Defense intends to reframe the current situation to redefine the "Defense model" and then adapt the reality of the "Defense function" to it, with a careful use of available resources, aiming to have motivated and trained personnel, efficient equipment, and 100% reserves

[150] From the 2003 budget these will be our guiding principles

[151] Parliament and the country will be involved in the decisions and informed about the actions needed to achieve the desired results

[152] The ultimate goal remains to provide Italy with a modern and efficient Armed Forces, an operational arm of Italy's policies, to contribute to the best of our ability to building a world where freedom, law, and justice reign everywhere

[153] Rome, December

[154] Antonio Martino Minister of Defense The book was edited by General Pietro Giannattasio, Head of the Office for Military Policy (an office in direct collaboration with the Minister of Defense), who was its inspiration

[155] The structure was modeled on that adopted in the 1985 volume

[156] The text is based on material provided by the General Staffs for the drafting of the individual sections and is intended to provide a snapshot of what existed on 18 October 2001, and therefore does not indicate subsequent developments

[157] General Pietro Giannattasio added, at my direction, his personal assessment of the possible evolutionary lines of Defense policy

[158] The essay, contained in the appendix, represents a valuable contribution provided by an authoritative expert who simply indicates the topics that could be the subject of further study in the future with the aim of increasing the efficiency of the operating units, while maintaining the organic volumes established by law

[159] The White Paper will be updated annually with a dossier reporting all the changes that have occurred in the meantime

[160] The Government's gratitude and my personal gratitude go to General Giannattasio and all those who made this meritorious work possible for their commitment

[166] Political-Military Relations 1.3.2 Disarmament and non-proliferation regimes - General - The CFE Treaty - The Vienna Document - The Stability Pact - The Ottawa Convention on the Prohibition of Anti-Personnel Mines - The Convention on the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons - Small Arms and Light Weapons (SALW) - The Open Skies Treaty - The NATO High Level Group - The NATO Senior Defence Group on Proliferation (DGP) - The Convention on the Prohibition of Biological Weapons (BIOLOGICAL WEAPON CONVENTION – BWC) Evolution of the geostrategic framework and the missions of the Armed Forces The fall of the Berlin Wall and the collapse of the Twin Towers have completely changed the fundamental parameters of the global strategic scenario

[167] The first of those events, twelve years later, can already be placed in some historical perspective

[168] The second announces a current event with consequences of extraordinary evolutionary significance

[169] Before 1989, the East/West opposition presented a threat of clear origin and of quantitative and qualitative scope that could be defined with appreciable precision

[170] It was a threat limited in its extreme consequences by the deterrence of a nuclear response, possible for both sides

[171] The end of bipolarism, and of the Cold War, did not create the conditions for the expected stability, but instead gave rise to new types of crises

[172] Following the eclipse of the bipolar order, the enthusiasm and the just and understandable hopes of the early days have faded, while all the difficulties inherent in the attempt to build a different international order—one that is freer, more democratic, and more respectful of human rights—have emerged forcefully

[173] Multiple factors of insecurity have appeared on the international scene, which have forced a radical rethinking of the defense models of Western societies, previously focused on the availability of arsenals calibrated to the old typical threat

[174] The immobility of the European scenario during the Cold War was replaced by a framework of instability and new security risks that pushed Italy, together with its European and Atlantic allies, to substantially rethink and redraw its military policy action

[175] Thus, in the last decade of the last millennium, the Atlantic Alliance underwent a profound process of reform

[176] The United States of America has reviewed its strategic priorities, its operational tools, and its international commitments

[177] The European Union is committed to developing its own common foreign, security and defence policy

[178] The Mediterranean, with its strong economic imbalances between north and south, its multiple conflicts and tensions, its centrality as an economic, civil, and military communication route, has assumed an increasingly greater strategic importance

[179] Eastern European countries are seeking a place in Europe and the world, firmly anchored in the West and its value system

[180] The current phase of the Euro-Atlantic security framework is the legacy of the transformations that took place within NATO and the EU in the final decade of the last century, a process in which Italy played a significant role, contributing to overcoming the old barriers that divided Europe and to modernizing the transatlantic bond, also expertly combining the strategic objectives of European integration with those of consolidating Euro-Atlantic spaces

[181] At the same time, an extraordinary effort to adapt by national and international defense organizations has led to a revision of strategic concepts and doctrines to address new threats that have become multifaceted, widespread, and multidirectional, requiring multidimensional and multinational responses

[182] The terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001, further disrupted previous geostrategic arrangements, projecting new risks onto the international scene deriving from possible terrorist and organized crime attacks

[183] The traditional threat no longer exists; local risks are emerging that base their capabilities not only on weapons, but also on more diversified and sophisticated tools, such as the movement of money or legal and illicit commercial goods, which allow for large profits, which can be used for criminal purposes

[184] This involves a multiplicity of asymmetric activities which, when combined and interconnected in various ways, create the risks that the international community will have to face in the future

[185] Terrorism is a catalytic and multiplying factor of these risks

[186] Security and defense policies today find themselves no longer limited to the traditional sphere of purely military capabilities, but must also confront a transversal enemy, often insidious and at times immaterial

[187] The evolution from that threat to these risks represents a real difference between what was and what is today a condition of systemic crisis, which negatively impacts the pursuit of the country's vital interests

[188] But the risks transcend national borders

[189] In an increasingly interconnected environment, the "amount of risk" accepted by a nation within international coalitions represents the risk shared by all

[190] Compared to the old threat, current risks, but also challenges and opportunities, are more complex and require broader and more diversified responses

[191] International action, in addition to traditional political, diplomatic, economic, cultural and cooperation instruments, is increasingly making active use of the military, which has become one of the essential indicators of the credibility and reliability of the country system in international relations

[192] This new geostrategic phase places European and allied military instruments before new operational needs and the necessity of acquiring the flexibility of use necessary to face new missions with continuously variable geometry

[193] The "missions" of our Armed Forces today are defined within a broad spectrum of operational actions aimed, in compliance with constitutional principles, at protecting national security, political and territorial integrity, the values of our civilization and economic and social well-being and development

[194] But the protection of national security today takes on a broader meaning that includes, in addition to the defense of national sovereignty, contributing to international stability and security, the legitimate safeguarding and protection of our interests as well as the prevention of old and new risks, and the fight against violations of law and peace

[195] Naturally, this concept is increasingly embedded in the actions of the major international organizations of which we are an active and responsible part, particularly the European Union, the Atlantic Alliance and the United Nations

[196] Consequently, support for the international community's operational missions has become, particularly in recent years, a defining element of the employment of our Armed Forces

[197] The new configuration of the global scenario therefore requires a continuous and careful reevaluation, first political and then strategic, of defense priorities also aimed at developing new military capabilities and new force systems, capable of addressing a diverse array of new risks

[198] The Italian Armed Forces are not shying away from this challenge, evolving from the predominantly static defense of sovereignty to dynamic support for the international community's efforts to prevent and manage crises. They are also enriching their professionalism, which must be disseminated at all levels as an essential guarantee for addressing the multiplicity of tasks. This commitment has developed in a context in which the country has recently demonstrated its ability to clearly identify its security interests, strengthening its national identity

[199] The guidelines of national and international Security and Defense Policy have, in fact, demonstrated a significant sharing of “bipartisan” choices and, therefore, more authoritative and credible in the international context

[200] The global picture and the actors of international politics

[201] UN, WEU, EU, NATO, OSCE General In this difficult decade marked by armed conflicts, wars and international crises that have tragically affected all continents, including Europe, new principles have slowly been asserting themselves within the International Community in ways that were unthinkable in the old system, even if they are still insufficient to define a new system of relations between States

[202] State sovereignty has ceased to be an absolute and incontestable value in the international legal system

[203] The belief has gradually gained ground that the international community has the right and duty to intervene in the internal affairs of a single state when it is responsible for serious and repeated human rights violations against its own citizens

[204] In such cases, the conduct of States appears in itself capable of creating a threat to international peace and security and cannot leave us indifferent

[205] On the other hand, the experience of recent years has clearly demonstrated that the violation of human rights is frequently connected with the violation of the right of peoples to identity and self-determination

[206] In such a changing geopolitical landscape, major international institutions have become increasingly aware of their role and responsibility in supporting peace, within a framework of complementarity and synergy between the contributions of individual member countries

[207] At the same time, international institutions have proven to be only partially capable of managing new crises and conflicts

[208] Italy is characterized, in the international context, by a strong presence in International Security and Defense Organizations

[209] Thanks to this significant participation in international initiatives, as well as a strong capacity for proposition, Italy has acquired growing global political weight and, from a “consumer” country of security, has become a “producer” country of security

[210] This policy is consistent with and substantiates the commitments undertaken and the role played within the United Nations, the European Union, the Atlantic Alliance, and the OSCE, the major international organizations upon which security, the foundation of well-being and national cohesion, is actively and responsibly based

[211] In summary, the principles that govern the national approach towards the various international actors are: participation in NATO, an organisation that remains the foundation of the continent's collective defence and the primary guarantee of the country's security

[212] • participation in the European Union in its role as a regional body for cooperation, development and security in and for Europe, as the European pillar of transatlantic security cooperation

[213] • recognition of the UN and the OSCE as bodies representing a global will and therefore sources of legitimacy for initiatives promoted at the regional level; • development of bilateral relations for common security, both within the aforementioned bodies, but also with those countries that are not members, particularly in the Mediterranean area. 1.2.2 The United Nations (UN) The UN is the first international institution of reference for its preeminent role in the prevention and political management of crises and in globally addressing new challenges and the increased risk of instability in various regions of the world

[214] This principle of primacy of the UN mandate derives from its universalism which gives it the necessary legitimacy and political authority

[215] But, despite this undisputed institutional and moral preeminence, the UN does not yet appear to have a sufficiently effective structure for the direct management of complex crises involving the use of military force

[216] The North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO), the bastion of our national defense during the Cold War, remains the linchpin of our security today, but in the new forms towards which the Atlantic Alliance is evolving, both in terms of missions and internal structures

[217] From a defense organization against the threat from the East, and therefore "exclusive", the Alliance has transformed itself, with a series of internal and external reforms, into a builder of Euro-Atlantic security, capable of projecting stability and security to the East and the South, and therefore "inclusive

[218] The transatlantic bond thus remains the foundation of Western security, in a context of accelerated transformation towards a more balanced and equitable relationship of responsibilities and duties between Europeans and the United States

[219] NATO's New Strategic Concept The evolutionary process that led to the definition of NATO's New Strategic Concept, finally finalized at the Washington Summit, began in the early 1990s with the "London Declaration", which initiated a project to adapt the organization's structures to the new security context resulting from the disappearance of the East-West confrontation

[220] To the dialogue-deterrence duo, a third fundamental element was added: cooperation with former adversaries, potential future partners, in the search for a new type of relationship that would guarantee the highest possible level of peace and stability in the Euro-Atlantic area

[221] The subsequent Rome Summit laid the foundations for a more institutional system of relations with the countries of Central and Eastern Europe, with the establishment of a forum, the North Atlantic Cooperation Council (NACC), which initially involved nine nations

[222] At the Brussels Summit in January 1994, the Partnership for Peace (PfP) initiative was launched, serving both as an instrument of cooperation and as a means of preparing and vetting candidate countries for the Alliance's eastward enlargement. This initiative consisted of an invitation, open to the states participating in the North Atlantic Cooperation Council (NACC) (later replaced in 1997 by the Euro-Atlantic Partnership Council (EAPC), and to other member states of the Conference on Security and Cooperation in Europe (CSCE) (later renamed OSCE), to join NATO countries in a program of practical cooperation aimed at strengthening their capacity to work together in peacekeeping, crisis management, and general humanitarian tasks

[223] Currently, this cooperative form, which benefits from the participation of 27 partner countries, in addition to those of the Alliance, can rightly be considered a fundamental component of security in the Euro-Atlantic area, a truly central point of NATO policy

[224] The “New Strategic Concept”, recognizing the security factor as intimately connected to political, economic and social considerations, based the existence of a collective defence capacity on dialogue and cooperation, to be achieved through collaboration with new partners in Central and Eastern Europe

[225] The concept of security needed to be understood in an even more global manner than in the past, encompassing risks of various kinds such as the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction and their means of delivery, the interruption of vital resource flows, and acts of terrorism and sabotage

[226] The most significant aspect of the New Strategic Concept consisted in the reworking of the tasks (fundamental security tasks

[227] with the confirmation of those relating to security, consultation and deterrence and defence, but with the elimination of that of the maintenance of strategic balances in Europe, considered no longer relevant

[228] Two new tasks have been added

[229] that of crisis management, to be carried out “on a case-by-case basis and by consensus of individual nations”, and that of cooperation with other countries in the Euro-Atlantic area (partnership

[230] Furthermore, in striving to achieve its purpose and fulfill its fundamental security tasks, the Alliance: recognizes the "authority of the United Nations Security Council and the responsibility of the OSCE for the maintenance of international peace and security"; reaffirms its willingness to intervene with its own procedures, while respecting the autonomous decisions of member states and in accordance with their respective constitutions. Following the definition of the New Strategic Concept, guidelines were drawn up for: the review of the Alliance's political and military structures and procedures; the reduction of Alliance forces and their response levels, with a restructuring based on the new crisis management and peacekeeping missions

[231] This brings us to Washington, where, in essence, NATO is redefining itself as an organization for the 21st century

[232] On this occasion, in fact, the “new” NATO sees the light

[233] The “new” NATO The process of “external adaptation” The key step in the reconfiguration of the Alliance towards external countries occurred with the Madrid Summit (July 1997), a true turning point for NATO policy

[234] During this Summit, the enlargement of the Atlantic Organization to new countries of Central and Eastern Europe (Czech Republic, Hungary, Poland) was formally launched, and the Charter for a specific Partnership with Ukraine was also signed

[235] In essence, these are two significant "external adaptation" moves that initiate a process that is not yet concluded

[236] Indeed, the “open door” principle underlines that the Alliance could extend future invitations to nations capable of assuming the responsibilities and obligations of membership

[237] To this end, NATO has established a programme of activities to assist aspiring countries, the Membership Action Plan (MAP), which offers aspiring countries a list of activities that can be used to support their preparation for possible membership in the Alliance

[238] Italy has based its policy on full support for the "open door," in particular by supporting the entry of those countries whose NATO membership could represent a driving force for achieving better social and economic goals, while also contributing to increased overall security

[239] The process of “internal adaptation”. In parallel with NATO's “external adaptation”, a process has developed, to make the Alliance more effective in the face of new types of threats

[240] An initial response to the need for a functional adaptation of the Alliance's military structure had already been made with the creation, in 1993, of the Combined Joint Task Forces (CJTF), a Multinational (Combined) and Joint Task Force organised and constituted to face Contingent Operations requiring Multinational Command and Control

[241] This idea, still under development, has been incorporated into a more general review process involving the command and force structures

[242] Review of the Command Structure Following the initiatives concerning the internal adaptation of the Alliance, initiated with the 1991 Strategic Concept and concretized in the “Long Term Study”, the need emerged for new and updated operational tools, to effectively and credibly carry out both the traditional defense missions of the member countries (operations under Article 5) and the new tasks, with particular reference to non-Article 5 missions - "Out of Area

[243] The mission, number, type and location of NATO Commands were therefore redefined, moving from a four-level command structure (for a total of 65 Headquarters, eight of which were on Italian soil) to a more streamlined organisation centred on 20 Commands

[244] As regards the Southern Region, the Regional Command of CINCSOUTH and the Sub-Regional Commands for air and naval assets in Naples (COMAIRSOUTH and COMNAVSOUTH) and a Sub-Regional Joint Command in Verona (JHQSOUTH) with a predominantly landbased presence were maintained on Italian territory

[245] NATO Command Structure - 2 Strategic Commands (SCs), SACLANT in the Atlantic (NORFOLK) and SHAPE (MONS) in Europe; - 3 Regional Commands (RCs) in the Atlantic (NORFOLK, NORTHWOOD and LISBON

[246] Regional Commands (RCs) in Europe (BRUNSSUM and NAPLES); " 7 joint Sub-Regional Commands in Europe, of which 3 in the Northern Region (HEIDELBERG, KARUP and STAVANGER) and 4 in the Southern Region (VERONA, MADRID, LARISSA and IZMIR

[247] Component Commands (CCs), one naval and one air, in the Northern European Region (NORTHWOOD and RAMSTEIN

[248] Component Commands, one naval and one air, in the Southern European Region, both in Naples

[249] Commands immediately subordinate to SACLANT and located in NORFOLK

[250] Atlantic Strategic Fleet Command (Strikfltlant); Atlantic Submarine Command (Subaclant

[251] NATO COMMAND STRUCTURE Review of Force Structure

[252] The NATO Force Structure Review (NFSR) process was initiated after the 1999 NATO Summit in Washington, with the aim of ensuring both an adequate reduction in the size of the Alliance's military instrument and the satisfaction of new strategic needs

[253] From this perspective, it was decided to abandon the traditional "mission oriented" structure and move towards a "capability oriented" structure

[254] Headquarters required for NATO Response Forces - three High Readiness Forces (L) HQs (HRF(L) HQs), predominantly land-based, with readiness ranging from 0 – 90 days

[255] six Forces at Lower Readiness HQs (FLR(L) HQs), predominantly land-based, with readiness ranging from 90 – 180 days

[256] a number of Longer Term Build-up Forces (LTBF) with readiness exceeding 365 days, necessary in the event of a "large-scale aggression" (Art. 5 operation); " three MCC (Maritime Component Command) or better HRF(M) HQs

[257] The project to revise the structure of the Forces is set in 4 phases

[258] After having passed the 1st (study phase) and the 2nd (bid analysis phase, completed with the issuance of the "Phase 2 Final Report", March 2001, with the acceptance of all valid proposals from HRF/FLR(L) HQs, the HRF (M) HQs under the new formula of Graded Readiness HQs), it has now entered the 3rd phase

[259] Finally, the actual implementation of the new structures will follow (4th and final phase). NATO's Defence Capabilities Initiative, launched at the Washington Summit, is a wide-ranging initiative, spurred by the glaring deficiencies highlighted by the armed forces of European partners during the recent Balkan crises

[260] It is intended to strengthen the Alliance's “European pillar” through a significant acceleration of the process of modernising operational capabilities

[261] Leveraging the support expressed at the highest political levels, NATO then launched a collective effort to stimulate and motivate, capable of consolidating synergies and guiding the costly process of adaptation that Europeans, to varying degrees, had already undertaken individually. A high-level political-military working group, the High Level Steering Group (HLSG), was established, led by the Secretary General, with the task of coordinating activities and presenting concrete results

[262] Five areas have been identified as "priority sectors for intervention", listed below: - mobility and risk management; - logistics sustainability

[263] effective engagement capability; - survivability of forces and infrastructure; - command and control

[264] These general areas have then been broken down into 59 specific implementing measures, for each of which solutions are studied, the costs are assessed, and the progress is monitored

[265] It is hoped that the strong political determination behind the initiative, the combined efforts, and the dialogue with partners, will help overcome the financial and bureaucratic obstacles that are hindering renewal everywhere

[266] The capability areas where the deficiencies appear most glaring at the strategic level are Command and Control of Forces (including the lack of airport radar), Intelligence and Strategic Transport (both air and sea

[267] Italy, considering the initiative to be of primary importance, has initiated the process of modernizing the Armed Forces towards the objectives of the DCI, prioritizing increased deployability and interoperability

[268] In Command and Control, the protected military communications satellite, SICRAL, was recently launched, which constitutes an essential component of any real and increased capability in the external theater force sector

[269] Regarding air and sea transport, the acquisition of dedicated aircraft and the construction of a major multipurpose naval unit capable of air and amphibious operations and the transport of men and equipment are important examples of our growing commitment in this sector

[270] The Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) The OSCE, which descends directly from the Final Act of the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe held in Helsinki in 1975, is the organization that brings together, within a new framework of pan-European cooperation, all 55 countries that were formerly adversaries during the Cold War

[271] It is the guarantor of the Treaty Publications Centre for Peace Studies www.studiperlapace.it ____________ CFE (Conventional Forces in Europe), signed in 1990 by the countries belonging to NATO and those of the Warsaw Pact, which represents the cornerstone of conventional disarmament on the Continent

[272] For twenty years, the OSCE has played a significant role in preventive diplomacy and the in-depth resolution of conflict causes, operating primarily in areas related to civil coexistence, such as monitoring the democratic nature of electoral and political-institutional, humanitarian and social processes, conflict prevention, and the restoration of post-conflict normality

[273] The CFE Treaty, the Code of Conduct, the Vienna Document 1999, the Charter for European Security, the management of disarmament agreements in the former Yugoslavia, and the study of new confidence- and security-building measures (CSBMs) are some of the concrete tools with which the OSCE develops its activity

[274] Italy participates in OSCE operations by sending numerous experts and with a financial contribution to long-term missions, exceeding 10% of the total

[275] The Western European Union (WEU

[276] Europe's evolutionary process in the field of security and defense has primarily involved the Western European Union, Europe's oldest post-war defense institution

[277] The definition of the WEU's role underwent a significant evolution in June 1992, when the so-called "Petersberg Declaration" was drafted, which entrusted it with the deployment of the armed forces of European nations for tasks known as "Petersberg missions," including humanitarian, peacekeeping, and crisis management activities. The creation of the European Union in November 1993 and the entry into force of the Maastricht Treaty subsequently led to the development of the "Common Foreign and Security Policy" (CFSP

[278] It has been defined as the “defense of the common values, fundamental interests and independence of the Union

[279] in maintaining peace and strengthening international security in accordance with the principles of the United Nations Charter

[280] in the development and consolidation of democracy and the rule of law and in the definition of a common defence policy, which could subsequently lead to a common defence”. This led to a redefinition of the WEU, foreseeing its development "as a defence component of the European Union and as a tool for strengthening the European pillar of the Atlantic Alliance”

[281] Ultimately, the WEU was to play a real “hinge” role between NATO and the EU

[282] Although the organisation's operational role was not considered "decisive", the WEU was credited with achieving important milestones such as the creation of common structures in satellite intelligence analysis, the development of a European security concept, the management of the first operations with international police forces and the creation of "multinational European forces

[283] This progress has paved the way for the EU's development in the field of Defence and Security, following a hereditary continuity criterion between the two institutions

[284] In 1997, the European Union, which had in the meantime established itself in the economic dimension and strengthened itself in the political one, began to assert itself as a new actor in the security of the Continent also thanks to the launch of the EuroMediterranean Partnership (Barcelona

[285] The inclusion of the Petersberg tasks in the Amsterdam Treaty laid the foundations for the decision at the 1999 Cologne European Summit to merge elements of the WEU into the European Union

[286] At the same time, the evolution of the transatlantic relationship has favored the emergence of the European Security and Defence Identity (ESDI

[287] Both of these steps require European countries to undertake a process of renewal and adaptation that requires them to assimilate and develop a culture of safety that is essential for managing new scenarios

[288] The European Union

[289] The evolutionary process of European Defence From the initial Treaty of Rome (25 March 1957) to today, the European Union has been able to create a community of economic and values

[290] Now, as we move towards progressive political integration, the Security and Defence Dimension plays an essential role and constitutes a powerful driver of integration and a driving force capable of supporting a common foreign policy for the future Europe

[291] This objective requires the availability of adequate operational capabilities to support policies to expand the framework of security, democracy and stability beyond the current borders of the Union

[292] An expansion that is fully in the interests of a highly industrialized country like Italy, for which the freedom and security of commercial and economic exchanges are a vital concern

[293] European Defence fits into both the Atlantic Alliance and the European Union

[294] For the first area, the reference framework is constituted by the decisions taken at the Atlantic Council in Berlin (3 June 1996) where it was agreed to support the development of a European Security and Defence Identity (ESDI) within the Alliance through the strengthening of a European pillar of NATO and the development of “separable but not separate military capabilities”

[295] For the second, the reference framework is represented by the Treaty of Amsterdam (2 October 1997) which established that the defence dimension is an integral part of the Union's action and of its Common Foreign and Security Policy (CFSP

[296] At the Washington Summit, on the 50th anniversary of NATO, (24 April 1999) it was reaffirmed that the development of the CFSP is compatible with the common concept of “Security and Defence Policy” and it was agreed to define and adopt the necessary arrangements, respecting the needs of NATO operations and the cohesion of its command structure, to: • ensure EU access to NATO planning capabilities that can contribute to the planning of EU-led operations; • provide for the availability to the EU of previously identified NATO common capabilities and assets for use in EU-led operations; • identify a range of European command options for EU-led operations; • further adapt the NATO defence planning system to more fully incorporate the availability of forces for EU-led operations

[297] Along the same lines, the WEU Ministerial Council in Bremen (10-11 May 1999) reconfirmed: • the willingness of European nations to strengthen their operational capabilities to carry out Petersberg-type missions, based on appropriate decision-making structures and making use of effective military resources within NATO or national or multinational resources outside the NATO structure; • the desire to further develop these structures and capabilities in complementarity with the Atlantic Alliance, avoiding unnecessary duplication

[298] • the need for the WEU to be operationally effective through the involvement and participation of all WEU countries, depending on their “status” and to continue cooperation with the EU and NATO

[299] The decisions of the European Council in Cologne (3-4 June 1999) on European defence, in June 1999, established the guidelines to enable the European Union to fully play its international role, giving it military capabilities to support the CFSP in the framework of peacekeeping missions (so-called Petersberg missions) and underlining that the Union's action in defence matters takes place "in accordance with the principles of the UN Charter

[300] At the Helsinki European Council (10-11 December 1999), the Union set itself the objective of having the capacity for autonomous action, supported by credible military forces and an adequate decision-making process

[301] Its Member States have committed to further developing a policy that will enable them to equip themselves with an efficient institutional framework to direct it, effective military capabilities to manage it, adequate financial resources to implement it, and a competitive and technologically advanced defense industrial base to support it

[302] Italy, one of the founding countries of the European construction process, must play a role commensurate with its political and economic potential

[303] Increasingly active participation in European and Atlantic bodies must therefore be accompanied by a coherent national policy to concretely implement the decisions that will gradually be made at EU level

[304] In particular, the following was agreed in Helsinki

[305] A common European Helsinki Headline Goal for readily deployable military capabilities will be defined, and targets for collective capabilities in the areas of command and control, intelligence, and strategic lift will be rapidly developed, to be achieved through coordinated national and multinational efforts, on a voluntary basis, to carry out the full range of Petersberg tasks. New political and military bodies will be established within the Council to enable the Union to take decisions on EU-led Petersberg operations and to ensure, under the authority of the Council, the necessary political control and strategic direction of such operations

[306] Principles for cooperation with third European NATO member states and other European partners in EU-led military crisis management will be agreed, without prejudice to the autonomy of EU decision-making processes

[307] The determination to carry out the Petersberg tasks will require Member States to improve national and multinational military capabilities, which will simultaneously strengthen NATO's capabilities where necessary and increase the effectiveness of the Partnership for Peace (PfP) in promoting European security

[308] Publications of the Peace Studies Centre www.studiperlapace.it The primary objective, “Headline Goal”, formulated at the Helsinki Summit, necessary to develop European capabilities can be stated as follows

[309] By 2003, through voluntary cooperation, the European Union should be able to rapidly deploy and sustain forces capable of carrying out all the Petersberg tasks in accordance with the Amsterdam Treaty, including the most ambitious ones, in operations at corps level (up to 15 brigades, or 50,000–60,000 men). These forces should be militarily autonomous and equipped with appropriate command, control, and information capabilities, as well as logistics, other war support units, and, where necessary, air and naval support elements

[310] Member States will need to be able to organise a full deployment at this level within 60 days, and in this context they will need to be able to provide smaller formations, ready to mobilise at very short notice for rapid intervention situations

[311] Member States must be able to sustain this deployment for at least one year, which will require an additional pool of deployable units (and supporting elements) with less rapid availability to replace the initial forces.”

[312] The subsequent European Council in Lisbon (22 May 2000) established a Committee with specific competence for the civilian aspects of crisis management and for the related strengthening and use of non-military instruments

[313] In line with these determinations, Italy—which attaches particular importance to the EU initiative—has offered a qualified conceptual contribution in the various sectors of intervention (police, civil protection, humanitarian aid, institutional reconstruction activities, electoral observers, administrative experts, etc

[314] At the European Council of Santa Maria di Feira (19-20 June 2000) it was decided to organize a capabilities commitment conference, with the intention of moving from a political objective to a precise military assessment of needs, on the basis of which each State can determine its own participation in the collective effort and from which the Fifteen will jointly identify the unsatisfied needs and the relative means to satisfy them

[315] The Feira Summit also defined the principles and modalities of agreements designed to enable European NATO members, which are not part of the EU, and other countries applying for membership to contribute to EU-led military crisis management

[316] Furthermore, the principles for consultation with NATO on military matters were defined and the following four priority areas were identified in which the EU will develop its relations with NATO: security issues; capability objectives; modalities for allowing the EU to access NATO assets; definition of permanent consultation mechanisms

[317] Furthermore, the Fifteen have set the objective of having, by 2003, on the basis of voluntary contributions from the Member States, 5000 police units to be assigned to international missions with the capacity to rapidly deploy 1000 men within thirty days

[318] With reference to the possible transition period between an initial military command and a subsequent civilian leadership, the line of establishing robust, rapidly deployable, flexible and interoperable European Union Integrated Police Units was approved, as well as the possibility of cooperation in this specific field between a small number of Member States

[319] In Feira, it was also clarified that Europe’s contribution to civilian crisis management can be expressed in response to requests from leading organizations such as the United Nations or the OSCE, or through actions conducted autonomously by the European Union itself

[320] The catalogue also covers collective capabilities, known as "key capabilities," which include intelligence, strategic transport, and command and control

[321] These capabilities are the subject of bilateral or multilateral partnerships within the EU and complement the land, naval and air capabilities in which the Fifteen have committed to participate

[322] The Force Commitment Conference (20 and 21 November 2000) in Brussels represented a further significant step forward in building a European Security and Defence Dimension. The day after the Force Commitment Conference, the Nice European Council (7-9 December 2000) took place, taking a series of important political decisions for the continuation of the CFSP plan

[323] These decisions concern

[324] the formalization of permanent structures

[325] Political and Security Committee, Military Committee and Military General Staff; • the launch of a civilian dimension to crisis management, through the creation of a rapid police intervention force of 5,000 men, 1,000 of whom can be deployed within 30 days (in this regard, the Carabinieri contribute approximately 800 men, placing them first among all European nations

[326] • the definition of permanent consultation procedures between the European Union and NATO

[327] • the integration of the WEU's own functions into the EU

[328] • agreements on the modalities of consultation and participation of potential partners (candidate countries for EU membership and European countries that are part of NATO but not of the EU

[329] In particular, the way was given to the establishment of permanent bodies responsible for playing, under the guidance of the High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy, a more active and responsible role in the field of security and crisis management

[330] The permanent Political and Security Committee (PSC), based in Brussels, composed of national representatives at senior official/ambassador level

[331] It is the forum for dealing with all matters relating to the CFSP

[332] In the event of military crisis management operations, the PSC shall ensure, under the authority of the Council, political control and strategic direction of operations; the Military Committee (MC), composed of the Chiefs of Defence Staff, represented by their military delegates

[333] It is a forum for providing military advice and recommendations to the PSC, as well as for ensuring military direction of the General Staff

[334] The CM President will participate in Council meetings when decisions with defence implications need to be taken; the Military Staff (MS), which operates within the Council, will provide military advice and support to the CFSP, including the conduct of EU-led military crisis management operations

[335] The General Staff will ensure early warning, situation assessment and strategic planning within the Petersberg missions, including the identification of national and multinational European forces. A concept for the deployment of European police forces was developed in Nice, including both civilian and military police forces, according to two scenarios

[336] the first, which aims to strengthen local police capacities with training, assistance, control and advisory missions

[337] the second - which corresponds to complex crises - provides for the use of EU police forces to replace local police forces in carrying out missions aimed at restoring public safety

[338] Future Developments of European Defence The Union, in developing a European Security and Defence Policy, faces a major integration challenge, equal in complexity and scope to that of the euro

[339] As the euro is fully integrated into the global economy, so European Security and Defence policy must be firmly interconnected with the security policy of the Atlantic Alliance

[340] two sides of the same coin, distinct but not separate, under penalty of losing the effectiveness and value of our own security and therefore of the process of European political integration

[341] The first of the main components in the process of building a Common European Security and Defence Policy is institutional leadership

[342] The final structure of the new institutional bodies created to manage this policy includes a significant role for the Political Security Committee (PSC

[343] It will be essential that this Committee has the capacity to become the steering body for crisis management and to establish effective interactions with the North Atlantic Council, thus ensuring a reliable and transparent relationship between the Union and the Alliance

[344] With regard to the specific implications inherent in decisions regarding the use of military force, the institutional direction for Europe must succeed in combining the unity of the overall Union framework with the specificity of security and defence policy compared to other Community policies

[345] The second component of the process concerns the reform of military instruments

[346] For them, there is a need for an organizational and doctrinal transformation and for the use of men and resources

[347] A transformation that requires a qualitative leap consistent with the ambitious yet realistic Helsinki objective, namely achieving adequate operational capacity by

[348] There is a very high degree of political support, among all, for the project of creating effective European military capabilities, coordinated and consistent with those of NATO, even among those countries traditionally considered more cautious by nature

[349] With reference to the initial objective set in Helsinki, a "Catalogue of Capabilities" has been prepared to face all types of crisis management missions, from strictly humanitarian ones to the more demanding ones of peacekeeping or peace enforcement

[350] In defining these capabilities – both quantitatively and qualitatively – the document outlines a coherent connection with the Defense Capabilities Initiative (DCI), decided by the Alliance at the 1999 Washington Summit. In defining national contributions to the common European objective, however, the shortcomings of European countries' operational capabilities emerged

[351] This "gap" between the required capabilities, defined in the Helsinki Catalogue, and those that Europeans are able to achieve today

[352] to make available to the Union, constitutes the challenge of making the Union's external action more credible, equipping it with effective decision-making and operational capacities

[353] These shortcomings have repercussions both on the process of building European Defence and on the European capabilities available to the Alliance

[354] In filling these gaps – as is necessary – each national contribution will therefore have a double value

[355] on the European and Atlantic sides, thus outlining a link between the two spheres, that of the Union and that of the Alliance

[356] The convergence between the operational objectives outlined in the European Defence Initiative and the Atlantic Alliance's "Defence Capabilities Initiative" ensures their integration into each other, according to the concept of "separable but not separate forces

[357] The areas in which to invest most decisively have been identified as interoperability, the availability of deployable forces on a professional basis, strategic mobility, command and control, communications, surveillance and intelligence, precision engagement, self-protection, and the ability to operate in environments at risk due to the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction

[358] The construction of European Defence cannot ignore the problem of adequate resources

[359] The effectiveness of military spending represents the third component in the process of building the European Security and Defence Policy

[360] European countries as a whole allocate approximately 60% of US military spending to defense, while the operational and projection capabilities of Europeans are far from being proportionate to this

[361] They represent only 10–15% of US capabilities

[362] It is easy to see how the cost of the lack of European convergence is equal to 50% of the missing capacities

[363] To this assessment we can add the estimate made by NATO military authorities, according to which the cost of the operational gap between the United States and EU countries would amount to approximately 30 billion dollars

[364] These estimates, although questionable in absolute terms, are indicative of a real, "political" as well as operational phenomenon

[365] The military gap between Europe and the United States is such that it is reflected in the real ability to decide and operate together

[366] In essence, the split in military capabilities risks turning into an operational and political split between the United States and Europe, which puts European security at risk

[367] A simple, reductive restructuring of European countries' forces, although necessary and underway, is not sufficient to modernize Europe's military capabilities and reduce the operational gap mentioned above

[368] European spending must certainly be optimised in all sectors, but it must also be increased in investments and advanced technologies

[369] The convergence process must guide us toward reducing the common factor costs present in each of our military instruments, the so-called "overheads", by concentrating and rationalizing the management structures supporting the operational forces, and progressively integrating military demand, both in terms of operational requirements and acquisition processes

[370] In this sense, the convergence of European defense policies is a necessity to meet modernization objectives both within NATO and Europe

[371] In this context, after having first defined a homogeneous framework for current European military spending, it might be appropriate and effective to outline guidelines for European countries' progressive alignment with certain qualitative standards for military spending, identifying indicators that outline convergence objectives

[372] Among these, the incidence of military spending in relation to GDP, the ratio between investment spending and operating expenses

[373] the percentage of expenditure dedicated to research and development

[374] per capita military spending levels

[375] the amount of professional forces available in relation to the size of the population

[376] These are all indicators for which there is currently strong heterogeneity among Europeans, even by one in five, and for which paths of convergence should be outlined that would facilitate the contribution of each European country to achieving the common goal of increased European military capacity

[377] Adopting convergence criteria for military spending, albeit in a flexible and non-rigidly prescriptive manner, as was the case with the single currency, would greatly facilitate the process of creating an effective European Security and Defence Policy

[378] It is with this in mind that discussion and appropriate decision-making processes on the concept of a European Defence convergence criterion must be promoted within European institutional bodies

[380] The link between foreign policy and defense policy has consequently become very close

[382] The network of international relations in which the Ministry of Defence participates is complemented by qualified support for the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in various negotiating forums for disarmament and non-proliferation (UN, OSCE, EU, NATO, Geneva Conference on Disarmament) and by the active and direct implementation of the Treaties and Conventions ratified by Italy (CFE

[383] The reduction of armament levels and verification measures resulting from arms control and non-proliferation agreements support NATO's political and military efforts to achieve its strategic objectives

[384] Of particular importance among these are the strengthening of stability on the European continent, made possible by the CFE Treaty, the substantial reductions in nuclear weapons made possible by the START treaties, the signing of the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty (CTBT), the automatic and unconditional renewal of the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT), the entry into force of the Chemical Weapons Convention (CWC), the aforementioned Ottawa Convention on the Ban of Anti-Personnel Mines, and other confidence- and security-building measures (CSBMs) developed by the OSCE which, while only politically binding, contribute to de-escalation in crisis areas

[385] This is because, despite the positive evolution of the strategic environment and the high improbability of a large-scale conventional aggression directed against the Alliance, the possibility of the emergence of such a threat in the long term persists
