[489] The Italian contribution to European defence 2.1 The chain of command 2.1.1 The Head of State The Constitution (art. 87), with regards to Defence, attributes the following powers to the President of the Republic: • the Command of the Armed Forces

[490] • the presidency of the Supreme Defense Council

[491] • the declaration of a state of war decided by the Chambers

[492] Regarding the actual command of the Armed Forces, although the doctrine seems to favor that this should be the responsibility of the Government, according to the guidelines and under the control of Parliament, it nevertheless recognizes that the command constitutionally conferred on the President of the Republic cannot have a purely ceremonial and symbolic character, also in light of the fundamental role of control and guarantee, recognized to the Head of State, of the use of the Armed Forces

[493] This role of ensuring constitutional balance in matters of defense and security policy is clearly strengthened by Law No. 25/1997, "Powers of the Minister of Defense and Restructuring of the Armed Forces and Defense Administration," which, by increasing and enhancing the Supreme Defense Council's responsibilities in matters of security and defense, also increases the political significance of the powers of the Head of State, as President of the institutional body

[494] The Supreme Defense Council The law establishing the Supreme Defence Council no. 624/1950 assigns to the Council the task of examining general, political, and technical issues pertaining to national defense and of determining the criteria and guidelines for organizing and coordinating activities that concern it in any way

[495] Subsequently, Law No. 25/1997 expanded the Council's powers by granting it the power to examine fundamental decisions regarding national security and strengthened its role as a liaison between constitutional bodies where security issues can be addressed and resolved

[496] Indeed, the Supreme Defence Council is the forum where, even in times of crisis, timely and in-depth information is provided to the President of the Republic on government decisions regarding defence. This enables him to act as swiftly and effectively as possible in ensuring compliance with the aims, means (particularly the military), and limits set by the Constitution. This ensures the ultimate subjection of the Armed Forces to the supreme political institutions of the Republic, guaranteeing their political neutrality, and ensuring their exclusive use in the service of the Nation

[497] In particular, the provision of the aforementioned Law no. 25/1997 that government resolutions on security and defense must be examined by the Supreme Council of Defense and approved by Parliament means that the President of the Republic exercises further control over this sensitive matter

[498] Furthermore, this appears to be in accordance with the composition of the body in which the Ministers responsible for strategic sectors of the Nation participate

[499] The Supreme Defense Council is chaired by the President of the Republic and has the following composition

[500] • President of the Council of Ministers, with functions of Vice President

[501] • Minister of Foreign Affairs; • Minister of the Interior

[502] • Minister of the Treasury; • Minister of Defense

[503] • Minister of Productive Activities

[504] • Chief of the Defence Staff

[505] The Supreme Council of Defense normally meets twice a year, however the President of the Republic may convene meetings whenever he deems it necessary, after consulting with the Prime Minister, or upon proposal of the Prime Minister

[506] At the request of the President's of the Republic, other Ministers, in addition to those indicated, other institutional officials of the State and of the Armed Forces, as well as individuals with particular expertise in the scientific, industrial and economic fields, may participate

[507] Parliament is the constitutional body that directly represents the will of the people

[508] The Constitution (Articles 56, 57, 70 and 71) gives Parliament a central position and role in the political-constitutional system, configuring it as the most important link between the community and its governments

[509] Its centrality in the constitutional system is demonstrated through its ownership of functions of pre-eminent importance, among which the fundamental ones are the legislative function and that of political direction and control of the Government

[510] It is clear that the two fundamental functions of Parliament are crucially and incisively integrated into the Government's general policy and therefore into that of State security

[511] In particular, with regard to security policy, the approval of Law No. 25/1997 appears to achieve at least four objectives: indicate a single person responsible for the operations of the Armed Forces - the Chief of Defence Staff - in order to allow the bodies that exercise the function of political-administrative direction or the legislative and direction and supervision functions to more quickly identify the various responsibilities; establish two matters (security policy and defence) for which the Government has political responsibility, in the sense that it is responsible for developing the objectives and programmes to be pursued in matters of defence and security and for outlining the related political, international, operational and financial consequences; make promptly known to the public those acts that are decisive for the life of the country and for the maintenance of its international relations; obtain parliamentary consent on government resolutions of great importance for the entire national community

[512] Furthermore, Parliament's involvement in government decisions on defense and security issues leads to a more shared political responsibility in making decisions that are crucial to the nation's future. It also helps establish a collaborative relationship between military leaders and political leaders that respects each other's expertise

[513] The President of the Council of Ministers The function of the President of the Council of Ministers, as can be seen from Article 95 of the Constitution, is to direct the activity of the Council of Ministers and to promote and coordinate that of the individual Ministers to ensure the implementation of the political and administrative guidelines established by the Council

[514] More specifically, and also in light of Law No. 400/1988, the main powers of the Prime Minister in matters of State security are

[515] • direct the general policy of the Government, for which he is responsible, to this end by drafting the programme and establishing the directives

[516] • coordinate the activities of individual Ministers in relation to acts concerning Government policy; • promote and encourage, including through directives, the Government's activities for the implementation of the agreed program

[517] Although Law 25/1997 assigns the entire Government the power to adopt resolutions on security and defense matters, the need for timely decisions regarding the protection of state security has tempered the principle of collegiality with the equally preeminent principle of monocracy, thus highlighting the role of the President of the Council of Ministers, that is, the body responsible for the general policy of the state

[518] The principle of monocracy in security and defense policy has been reaffirmed by constitutional jurisprudence itself

[519] In fact, the Constitutional Court has significantly affirmed that political activity aimed at the internal and external defense of the State must also be considered to be within the competence of the President of the Council of Ministers

[520] On the basis of this ruling by the Constitutional Court, the legislator has explicitly provided for the President of the Council of Ministers, with regard to "internal" and "external" aspects of security, the attribution of the senior management of general political responsibility and the coordination of information and security policy in the interest and for the defense of the State (Law No. 801 of 24 October 1977, establishing the information and security services

[521] The Minister of Defense (fig

[522] The Minister of Defense, pursuant to the provisions of Law No. 25 of February 18, 1997, "Powers of the Minister of Defense, Restructuring of the Armed Forces and Defense Administration Leadership" and Presidential Decree No. 556 of October 25, 1999, "Implementing Regulation of Article 10 of Law No. 25 of February 18, 1997, concerning the powers of military leadership

[523] • implements the resolutions on defense and security adopted by the Government, submitted to the Supreme Defense Council for examination and approved by Parliament; • issues directives regarding military policy, intelligence and security activities and technical-administrative activities

[524] • approves the joint general and operational planning with the resulting technical-financial programs as well as the planning relating to the industrial area, both public and private, of interest to the defense

[525] • issues directives on communication, public information and promotional activities for the Armed Forces; gives general directives to the Chief of Defence Staff: on the relations he must maintain with the corresponding Military Authorities of other countries regarding military problems of common defence; on the national direction he must represent at the high military councils established within the framework of international defence agreements

[526] on the formulation by the Chief of Defence Staff of joint planning directives for the use, logistical support and multinational training, and of the resulting international technical-operational programs and agreements, taking into account the commitments undertaken; on the preparation and management of memoranda of understanding and international inter-force technical agreements having operational and/or training implications; on the transfer of Armed Forces resources and materials

[527] with regard to countries with which bilateral or international agreements exist for any reason; • establishes, with regards to the technical-administrative and technical-industrial area

[528] the directives relating to scientific research of interest to the Armed Forces

[529] the political-administrative and high-level administration guidelines regarding the technical-industrial and technical-administrative areas of Defence; • provides national guidance in the field of technical-scientific activities for defence purposes; • represents in high international forums within the framework of the implementation of multinational agreements

[530] • avails itself of the high-level consultancy of the Supreme Council of the Armed Forces for all matters provided for by law

[531] To carry out its duties, it receives from the Chief of Defence Staff: • information on the strategic operational situation of national interest and on foreseeable developments; • information on the efficiency of the military instrument, on the need for human, material and financial resources to achieve the pre-established objectives

[532] • proposals and provisions relating to the general financial planning of the military instrument

[533] • proposals on joint operational planning and the resulting technical-financial programs

[534] • general guidelines for the organization of each Armed Force

[535] • distribution of military and civilian personnel resources to be assigned to the technical-operational bodies as well as that of military personnel to be assigned to the technical-administrative and technical-industrial bodies of Defence

[536] from the Secretary General National Director of Armaments: • proposals regarding actions aimed at harmonizing the objectives of Defense with national economic-industrial and technical-scientific policy

[537] • proposals on the general lines of the organisation of the bodies in the relevant technical administrative and technical-industrial areas

[538] • technical-industrial consultancy elements relating to the production of defence materials within the framework of the armaments policy for which it is responsible

[539] Publications Peace Studies Centre www.studiperlapace.it The entire set of provisions indicated above are placed in the "Ministerial Directive" on the basis of which the Chief of Defence Staff issues the "Strategic Concept" where the directives of the Minister of Defence are concretely implemented

[540] In short, according to the democratic principle, the military leadership depends on the political leadership and is responsible for its actions to the political leadership

[541] The current restructuring of the Ministry of Defence largely dates back to November 1986, when the then Minister of Defence Giovanni Spadolini presented to the Senate a draft bill aimed at revising the Ministry's top management structure in a unified manner, assigning very specific responsibilities to the political and military levels

[542] In fact, the Chief of Staff of Defence was no longer expected to be "primus inter pares", but hierarchically superior to the Chiefs of Staff of the Armed Forces and to the Secretary General of Defence and National Director of Armaments, with the latter being limited to technical-operational responsibilities

[543] As is known, it took ten years and four legislatures to complete this reform which, although modified in some points, still retains the basic approach it had at the beginning

[544] The Armed Forces today are defined as one of the instruments that the Government uses to implement its policies

[545] The Military Instrument, therefore, must be adequately structured and prepared to carry out the tasks assigned to it

[546] These duties are defined in Law No. 331 of November 14, 2000, containing the "Rules for the Establishment of Professional Military Service" and are structured as follows: the Armed Forces are at the service of the Republic; the organization and activities of the Armed Forces comply with Articles 11 and 52 of the Constitution and the law; the primary task of the Armed Forces is the defense of the State; the Armed Forces also have the task of operating for the purpose of achieving peace and security, in accordance with the rules of international law and the decisions of the international organizations to which Italy belongs

[547] The Armed Forces contribute to the protection of free institutions and carry out specific tasks in circumstances of public disasters and in other cases of extraordinary necessity and urgency

[548] In reality, the changing international landscape, the sudden crisis situations that arise, the various hotbeds of tension that arise in areas of priority national strategic interest, but also in other geographical zones where Italy has found itself working to support peace and human rights, had already led successive Ministers of Defense since the fall of the Berlin Wall to propose successive restructurings of the Armed Forces in light of the criterion, also followed by other nations, of reducing quantity in favor of quality

[549] The initial trigger for the latest changes was promoted by Law No. 549 of 28 December 1995, linked to the 1996 Budget Law. Article 1 of the Law set out the guiding principles and criteria to be followed in implementing the subsequent specific delegation granted to the Government regarding the reorganization of military structures

[550] Consequently, "drafts" of legislative decrees were prepared which essentially refer to

[551] • reduction and reorganization of the number of territorial operational commands and peripheral Defense structures

[552] • differentiation and expansion of activities aimed at civil protection and environmental protection

[553] Publications of the Peace Studies Center www.studiperlapace.it ____________ • establishment of the Joint General Staff Institute; • reorganization of the central area of the Ministry of Defense

[554] • redetermination of the organic staffing of the civilian personnel of the Ministry of Defence and the related mobility

[555] • disposal of structures and properties no longer used

[556] • restructuring of arsenals, factories and technical centres

[557] All this occurred without an initial definition of the reference “defense model,” meaning that many legislative provisions had to undergo subsequent amendments, to the point that even today the final goal is not fully outlined

[558] Upon completion of the preparation of the aforementioned legislative decrees, the "drafts" were submitted to the required consultation with the trade unions, which resulted in the signing of two memoranda of understanding

[559] Subsequently, the aforementioned Legislative Decrees were forwarded to both houses of Parliament for consideration

[560] At the same time, Law No. 25, entitled "Reform of Military Leadership," was approved on February 18, 1997. This specifically addressed the responsibilities of the Minister of Defense, the Chief of the Defense Staff, the Secretary General of Defense and National Director of Armaments, and the Chiefs of Staff of the individual Armed Forces

[561] Army, Navy and Air Force

[562] The succession of Legislative Decrees In particular, with Legislative Decree no. 264 of 16 July 1997, the reorganization of the central area of the Ministry of Defence was established, in order to simplify the difficult relationships between the General Directorates, the Central Offices and the General Staffs

[563] The Decree has essentially halved the organizational structures of the central area of the Ministry, with the reduction of General Directorates from 19 to and Central Offices from 5 to

[564] The latter, the Central Office of Budget and Financial Affairs (BILANDIFE) and the Central Office for Administrative Inspections (ISPEDIFE), were placed under the direct control of the Minister, while the abolition of the Central Office for Military Equipment (ALLESDIFE), the Central Office for Organization, Methods, Mechanization and Statistics (ORMEDIFE), and the Central Office for Legal Studies and Legislation (LEGGIDIFE), resulted in the transfer of responsibilities to the Office of the General Secretariat (SEGREDIFESA) and the Minister's Cabinet (DIFEGABINETTO), respectively, for LEGGIDIFE

[565] Legislative Decree No. 265 of July 16, 1997, issued new regulations regarding civilian personnel and established the mechanisms for the redeployment of personnel

[566] Legislative Decree no. 459 of November 28, 1997, established the criteria for the organizational and functional reorganization of the technical-industrial area

[567] In practice, the 35 sector bodies have been reduced in staff numbers by approximately 5,000 units with the aim of providing the entire sector with a concrete rationalization and significant streamlining

[568] Furthermore, in accordance with the delegation granted to the Government by Law no. 662/96, Legislative Decree no. 490 of 30 December 1997 was promulgated, which provides for a general revision of the existing body of legislation regarding the recruitment, legal status, and advancement of Officers

[569] All this within a framework of strict inter-force homogeneity and a concrete reduction in personnel

[570] Legislative Decree no. 464 of 28 November 1997 reorganized the technical-operational area into its command, operational, logistical, and educational-training components

[571] Therefore, this Decree is considered one of the main provisions of the reform, because it determines - after more than thirty years - a drastic reduction in the technicaloperational area of Defense

[572] defines the measures for the suppression, revision and adaptation of the Commands/Entities of the territorial, operational and training Organization of each individual Armed Force and joint forces, reducing, among others, the number of Territorial Military Commands of the Armed Forces (Military Region Commands for the Army, Commands in Chief of the Maritime Military Department for the Navy, Air Region Commands for the Air Force); seeks to pursue a better overall balance of the operational instrument in its various components and articulations, attempting to achieve a qualitative improvement of the forces and an increase in the capacity for external projection, with accentuated "response" readiness, high autonomy and logistical sustainability, in line with the force structure defined in the new NATO doctrine

[573] tends to simplify the organization of the operational, logistical and educational training Command, providing, among others, for a joint operational command (COI) and operational commands of the Armed Forces, delegating to the logistics commands/inspectorates and commands/inspectorates responsible for the educational training function functions that were previously the responsibility of the General Staffs; • establishes the Higher Institute of the Joint General Staff, replacing the Higher Courses of the Armed Forces General Staff, with the task of perfecting the professional training and cultural preparation of the Officers of the Armed Forces

[574] • prepares the regulatory bases for civil protection and environmental protection activities

[575] Subsequently, 31 months later, in light of the lessons learned from the previous Legislative Decree, and in the presence of specific legislative delegation, a further Legislative Decree no. 214 of 21 May 2000 was issued, "Corrective and supplementary provisions of Legislative Decree no. 464 of 28 November 1997 containing structural reforms of the Armed Forces, pursuant to art. 9, paragraph 2 of Law no. 78 of 31 March

[576] This legislative act concerned the operational bodies of the Army, Navy, and Air Force and was intended to further eliminate duplication of effort and the waste of energy resulting from the different organization, preparation, and deployment of the individual Armed Forces, and to ensure adequate military organization to meet the needs of joint planning and integrated direction and management of the instrument. This final regulatory measure, more specifically, affected the so-called Peripheral High Commands of the Armed Forces, with particular reference to the Army (Military Regional Commands) and the Air Force (Air Regional Commands), redistributing their extensive logistical, administrative, garrison, infrastructural, and conscription and recruitment responsibilities among a small number of newly created Inspectorates/Commands responsible for a single function at the national level

[577] Also in the year 2000, on the basis of Law No. 380 of 20 October 1999, which established the possibility for Italian citizens to participate, on a voluntary basis, in competitions for the recruitment of Officers, Non-Commissioned Officers in permanent service and voluntary service soldiers, in the Armed Forces and the Guardia di Finanza, Legislative Decree No. 24 of 31 January 2000 was issued

[578] This regulated recruitment, legal status and advancement for women's military service

[579] All of this is primarily inspired by the implementation of the principle of equal opportunities in recruitment and access to different ranks, qualifications, specializations, and positions

[580] In this way, the aim was to formalize the regulatory support necessary to sustain the future developments of the "Defense panorama" and the four pillars that support it

[581] the reform of the top management, the reform of the personnel, the restructuring of the operational tool and the streamlining of the technical-administrative and technical-logistical support areas

[582] The entire set of regulations had meanwhile been further clarified by Presidential Decree no. 556 of 25 October 1999, "Implementation Regulation of Article 10 of Law no. 25 of 18 February 1997, concerning the powers of Military Higher Education," particularly with regard to the responsibilities and powers of military high-level officials, which were further clarified in the combined provisions of the two provisions in question

[583] The Chief of the Defence Staff The Chief of the Defence Staff

[584] • depends directly on the Minister of Defence, of whom he is the senior technical-military advisor, and to whom he is responsible for the implementation of the political-military guidelines received regarding the planning, preparation and use of the military instrument

[585] • proposes to the Minister the general financial and operational joint planning, as well as the consequent technical-financial programs, after consulting the Chiefs of Staff of the Armed Forces

[586] presents to the Minister of Defense the strategic operational situation of national interest and foreseeable developments; • reports to the Minister of Defense on the efficiency of the military instrument, indicating the human, material and financial resources required to achieve the established objectives

[587] • proposes to the Minister the general guidelines for the organization and distribution of military and civilian personnel resources within the technical-operational, technical-administrative and technical-industrial areas

[588] • defines the overall operational and technical-financial priorities; • issues inter-force directives concerning logistics, transport and military healthcare

[589] proposes to the Minister of Defence, after consulting the Chiefs of Staff of the Armed Forces, the general lines of organisation of each Armed Force

[590] • issues directives concerning mobilization and related escorts

[591] In the financial sector, the Chief of Defence Staff: • exercises operational control of funds allocated for investment; • exercises operational control of funds allocated to the operational sector; • issues directives for the operational use of investment funds, exercising this through the Secretary General of Defence and the Chiefs of Staff of the Armed Forces

[592] With regard to the employment of personnel, the Chief of Defence Staff: • designates, on the basis of proposals made by the Chiefs of Staff of the Armed Forces, the Officers assigned to joint, international and other Ministries positions, informing the Minister as appropriate; • defines the general criteria for employment within the Armed Forces; • provides instructions to the Minister, after consulting the Chiefs of Staff of the Armed Forces, regarding the assignment of Lieutenant Generals or corresponding ranks to the various positions within each Armed Force

[593] With regard to the use of forces as a whole, the Chief of Defence Staff, on the basis of the Minister's directives

[594] • establishes operational objectives, those of intelligence gathering, training and exercises, verifying the operational capabilities of the Armed Forces; • exercises Operational Command of operations and exercises both nationally and internationally, making use of the Joint Operations Commander

[595] In particular, for information activities, it oversees the relevant activities using the specific department that has assumed the functions of the dissolved departments (SIOS) of the Armed Forces

[596] The Secretary General of Defense and National Director of Armaments: • reports directly to the Minister of Defense for administrative responsibilities and to the Chief of Staff of Defense for technicaloperational responsibilities; • exercises the responsibilities inherent to the senior administration of the technical-administrative and technical-industrial areas, based on the directives received from the Minister to whom he is responsible for their implementation; • proposes actions to harmonize the objectives in the fields of research and development, production and procurement of weapons systems, vehicles and equipment both nationally and internationally

[597] • directs, directs and coordinates the activities of the General Directorates, issuing rules and directives for uniform conduct

[598] Within the financial sector, the Secretary General/National Director of Armaments, on the basis of the directives of the Chief of Defence Staff, exercises: operational control of the funds allocated to the functioning of the technical-administrative and industrial area, of which he also holds and exercises operational use, including those allocated to cooperation and international agreements

[599] • The operational use of the funds allocated to the joint research and development sectors and investment in the technical-administrative and industrial area

[600] With regard to the use of personnel, the Secretary General/National Director of Armaments proposes to the Chief of Defence Staff the qualitative and quantitative requirements for the personnel to be assigned to the General Secretariat, the General Directorates, and the joint bodies of the technical-administrative and industrial areas

[601] Finally, regarding the use of forces, based on the provisions of the Chief of Defence Staff, it issues directives for defining activities related to militarization and civil mobilization, relating to the technical-administrative and industrial areas

[602] The Chiefs of Staff of the Armed Forces: • depend directly on the Chief of Defence Staff, to whom they are responsible for the implementation of the directives and provisions received; • exercise the command function of the respective Armed Force; • are responsible for the organisation, preparation, training and logistics of the respective Armed Force

[603] In the financial sector, the Chiefs of Staff of the Armed Forces, on the basis of the directives issued by the Chief of Defence Staff, exercise: • operational control of the funds allocated to the operational sector of the respective Armed Force, of which they also hold and exercise the operational use, with the power to provide for the administration of those allocated to the efficiency of the means and materials with powers similar to those of the General Directors; • the operational use of the funds allocated to the investment sector of the respective Armed Force

[604] With regard to the employment of personnel, the Chiefs of Staff of the Armed Forces: • propose to the Chief of Defence Staff the Officers destined to hold positions in the joint, international and other Ministries, as well as the Lieutenant Generals or equivalent to be assigned to the various Armed Forces positions; • designate, giving prior notice to the Chief of Defence Staff, the General Officers or Admirals with a rank not higher than Major General or equivalent, to be assigned to the various positions within the respective Armed Forces; • provide for the handling of matters relating to the employment of Officer, Non-Commissioned Officer and Enlisted Personnel of the Armed Forces, without prejudice to the powers of the Chief of Defence Staff, and carry out the related administrative acts

[605] Finally, regarding the use of forces, within the scope of the exercise of the command function of one's Armed Forces and in accordance with the provisions issued by the Chief of Defence Staff

[606] • define the training activities of the respective Armed Force; • ensure, for the exercise of national and multinational joint operations and exercises, the qualitative and quantitative availability of the operational departments; • direct and conduct, with the help of the subordinate operational Commanders, the operations and exercises of interest to the respective Armed Force

[607] The General Commander of the Carabinieri: reports to the Chief of Defence Staff for the performance of military duties

[608] He is also invested with operational, training, and technical logistical responsibilities, in matters of recruitment, status, advancement, and employment, in line with the provisions of the "law on defense leaders" and the subsequent "implementing regulation

[609] With regard to the financial and administrative sectors, the General Commander is responsible for both the activities of the Central Body (Planning Body, General Directorate and Administrative Responsibility Centre) and the so-called "decentralised" activities (specific to the Territorial Military Command), hence the dual role that characterises his legal-administrative role

[610] The General Commander also defines the organizational and operational policies necessary to achieve the institutional objectives

[611] It therefore has all the policy, administrative and management tools allocated within the General Command

[612] The Committee of Chiefs of Staff (composed of the Secretary General of Defence and National Director of Armaments, the Chiefs of Staff of the Air Force, and the General Commander of the Carabinieri) is an advisory body to the Chief of Staff who chairs the said high council

[619] SISMI The entire restructuring process could not fail to also impact information and security activities, although to a lesser extent, since the basic system, that relating to SISMI, has not undergone any changes

[620] It is therefore confirmed that the assessment of the threat framework for Italy is institutionally entrusted to the Military Security Intelligence Service (Law 24 October 1977 no. 801 "Institutions and regulations of the intelligence and security services and regulation of state secrets

[621] SISMI carries out all intelligence and security tasks for the military defense of the independence and integrity of the State from any danger, threat, or aggression

[622] For the aforementioned purposes, SISMI also carries out counter-espionage tasks (art. 4 of law no

[623] In essence, SISMI represents a defence instrument and its activity: • concerns the military sphere, taking into account the extension that this concept has undergone with respect to the global defence of the State, also including sectors such as the political-military, economic, industrial, technological, scientific research sectors which have direct implications on military potential

[624] • it is aimed on the one hand at acquiring information that may have an impact on the defence of the State and on the other at preventing access to the information services of other States (counter-espionage

[625] In this regard, it is important to emphasize that some states use their intelligence services as an offensive tool of "indirect strategy," the dynamics of which are not limited to military espionage but, above all, reveal forms of political, industrial, or technological espionage, or subversion, sabotage, disinformation, penetration of the Armed Forces, and manipulation of social groups

[626] The counterintelligence activity conducted by SISMI aims to prevent all forms of indirect strategies applied against the Italian state and its institutions, and in any case to prevent them from achieving their objectives

[627] The President of the Council of Ministers is entrusted with the supreme direction, general political responsibility, and coordination of information and security policy in the interests and for the defense of the democratic State and the institutions established by the Constitution at its foundation (Article 1 of Law No

[628] The Minister of Defense, to whom SISMI depends, establishes its organization and oversees its activities based on the directives and provisions of the President of the Council of Ministers

[629] SISMI is required to communicate to the Minister of Defense and the Executive Committee for Information and Security Services (CESIS) all information received or in any case in its possession, the analyses and situations elaborated, the operations carried out and everything pertaining to its activity (Article 4 of Law No

[630] SISMI's activity is carried out exclusively within the framework of the directives received from the political authorities and another important aspect of it is represented by the elaboration of analyses and situations

[631] Every decision-making act must be supported by reliable information

[632] The more realistic the decision, the greater the availability of reliable information

[633] Mistakes in the assessment of information can lead political authorities to make decisions that are irrelevant to the defense of the State

[634] These considerations underscore not only the delicate task of gathering, evaluating, and interpreting the vast mass of information made available by modern research and communication tools, but above all they highlight the professionalism, experience, culture, intellectual rigor, and moral rectitude that are the hallmarks of Intelligence and Security Services personnel

[635] An Interministerial Committee for Information and Security has been established at the Presidency of the Council of Ministers to provide advice and make recommendations to the President of the Council of Ministers on the general directions and fundamental objectives to be pursued within the framework of information and security policy

[636] The Committee is chaired by the President of the Council of Ministers and is composed of the Ministers of Foreign Affairs, the Interior, Justice, Defense, Productive Activities, and Finance (Article 2 of Law No

[637] The Government reports to Parliament every six months, with a written report, on the information and security policy and on the results achieved

[638] A Parliamentary Committee consisting of four deputies and four senators appointed by the Presidents of the two houses of Parliament, on the basis of the criterion of proportionality, exercises control over the application of the principles established by this law (Article 11 of Law No

[643] The SIS (Information and Security Department) With the law on the restructuring of the Armed Forces' top management (law 25/97) and, subsequently, with the provisions of Presidential Decree 556/99 (Implementation Regulation), the SIOS (Operational and Situation Information Services) of the Armed Forces were disbanded and the information activity was brought to the joint level at the Defence General Staff

[644] The transfer of responsibility was sanctioned by the Minister of Defense's directive no. 1/30863/14.1.8/97 dated 15 May 1997 and the activity, after an experimental phase, took on a definitive configuration on 1 September 2000 with the establishment of the Information and Security Department and the dependent Joint Intelligence Centre and Joint Intelligence/Electronic Warfare School

[722] The General Directorate absorbed the pre-existing General Directorates of the Commissariat and General Services, taking over their respective responsibilities in the areas of study, development, procurement, distribution, support and disposal in the sectors of: food; fodder; clothing; barracks equipment and materials, and the acquisition of transport, labour, catering, cleaning services, etc

[950] The Educational and Training Organization

[951] As part of the reorganization of the Armed Forces, the reconfiguration of the School-Training Area has taken on particular importance, following both the pressing need to update personnel education and training cycles and the need to move beyond the logic of in-depth initial preparation with a few "refresher" sessions, and towards ongoing training, congenial to the application of increasingly complex and sophisticated training methods

[952] To achieve these results, both the training sector of the permanent active service categories and the scholastic-training sector responsible for the qualification/specialization of all personnel of all ranks of the Army have been affected by changes

[953] First of all, the Inspectorate for Training and Specialization (Rome) was recently established, responsible for the basic training, specialization, and subsequent qualification of all Armed Forces personnel

[954] It was established through the merger of the pre-existing Inspectorates of Weapons and Schools and directs the activities of all the Schools for Officers, Non-Commissioned Officers and Volunteers of the Army

[955] The Training Inspector, in addition to the Inspectorate staff, has under his command the training bodies listed in the table below

[956] The total personnel is 2065 officers, 2136 noncommissioned officers, 9906 enlisted men and 815 civilians

[957] The Logistics Organization

[958] Among the functional sectors of the Armed Forces that have been most revised, the logistics organization must be mentioned, which has undergone a profound transformation, from a static, largely territorial organization aimed at well-defined employment hypotheses, to a streamlined organization, with an integrated, efficient, and well-defined chain of command and control, ready to support the multiple forms of employment that can today be attributed to the Armed Forces

[959] In this context, it was decided to redefine the top of the Command and Control chain of the logistics organization, which sees three fundamental actors reporting to the Chief of Staff, each of whom has very distinct tasks and responsibilities: • the Logistics Department of the SME, essentially responsible for policy functions, i.e. the preparation of financial planning proposals for modernization and renewal, as well as the subsequent implementation of the programs through the definition of the technical-operational requirements of the new materials, development, testing, technical-operational evaluation and the assignment of mandates to the General Directorates responsible for procurement; • the Army Logistics Inspectorate, responsible for all management activities, both at central level, also through the resources of the pre-existing Logistics Corps Commands, later incorporated into Departments of the Inspectorate, and on the territory; • the Land Operational Forces Command

[960] In the new organizational structure, the Inspectorate certainly constitutes a key role, enabling the Operational Forces to express the appropriate capacity, in terms of efficiency, by deploying modular capacity structures, deployable in any eventuality, especially for interventions abroad or "out of area", and expandable without problems, also through the inclusion of support components provided by other Armed Forces

[961] or from allied or friendly countries

[962] In particular, ISPEL is responsible for identifying, procuring, and assigning the resources necessary for logistical support, both during operations and during training and stationary operations, issuing relevant directives to the Commander of Land Operational Forces, and planning home supplies for users

[963] By virtue of this, the logistics organization has been divided into two bands: adherence logistics, intended to directly support the operational component with deployable executive bodies, entrusted to the responsibility of the Commander of the Land Operational Forces; support logistics, intended to indirectly support the entire Armed Forces, operating with executive bodies located in the Motherland, the responsibility of which falls to the Army Logistics Inspector

[975] The foundation of the organization's operation is the desire to implement logistical support that is no longer "just in case," which presupposes preparing or carrying out everything that might be needed, with a great expenditure of resources and energy, but rather "just in time" logistical support, such as providing only what is needed and at the desired time, making use of the most modern management systems for all sectors and for all activities, from supplies to maintenance

[1026] The naval units and departments under its command are grouped into a number of complex commands

[1027] The restructuring of CINCNAV was inspired by three concepts

[1028] l consistency with the new NATO command structure, which led to the abolition of the fourth-level commands, to which CINCNAV belonged as the Central Mediterranean Command-in-Chief (COMEDCENT); l the concentration, at command levels dependent on CINCNAV, of all offshore naval forces, underwater units, mine countermeasures forces, coastal forces, amphibious forces, and fixed- and rotary-wing aircraft; l the transfer of operational functions and related assets previously entrusted to peripheral territorial commands, with the exception of those of units operating locally for headquarters needs

[1029] The only exception to this concentration of operational skills is the special forces (essentially, the Underwater and Raider Group, based in Varignano, La Spezia, which by their nature remain directly under the command of the Chief of Staff of the Navy

[1030] CINCNAV is also able to perform control functions for joint, multinational, or joint/combined operations, and could also find itself, in the event of a crisis or armed intervention, acting (similar to its counterparts in the Army and Air Force) under the CSd as ComFor specifically constituted for a specific need and/or having the CSd delegate the conduct of operations

[1068] The peripheral/territorial organization

[1069] The national territory, with particular reference to the coastal regions where the naval bases and other infrastructures of primary interest for the Navy are located, falls under the jurisdiction of six Peripheral High Commands, consisting of three Maritime Military Departments (MARIDIPART) and three Autonomous Maritime Military Commands (CMMA, each with its own name relating to the geographical area of interest

[1070] The Maritime Military Departments are those of the Upper Tyrrhenian, with headquarters in La Spezia (MARIDIPART LA SPEZIA), of the Adriatic, with headquarters in Ancona (MARIDIPART ANCONA) and of the Ionian and Strait of Otranto, with headquarters in Taranto (MARIDIPART TARANTO

[1071] They are joined by the Autonomous Maritime Military Commands of Sicily (also commanded by an Admiral), with headquarters in Messina (MARISICILIA), of Sardinia, with headquarters in La Maddalena (MARISARDEGNA) and of the Capital (MARICAPITALE), with headquarters in Rome

[1072] These bodies are responsible for controlling the Commands/Entities within their respective territories and the naval units permanently or temporarily under their control, and exercise their authority with respect to specific functions (for example, Schools, Arsenals, etc.). [1135] The Carabinieri 2.3.7.1 Restructuring The characteristics, tasks, prerogatives and dependencies of the Carabinieri are today essentially defined in Law 78 of March 2000 and in the articles still in force of the Organic Regulations of

[1136] In summary, the Force has the rank of AF and is a Police Force with general competence and in permanent Public Safety service

[1137] As an Armed Force, the Corps has an autonomous position within the Ministry of Defense, with organizational guidelines that establish the General Commander's dependence on the Chief of the Defense Staff for the fulfillment of military tasks, precisely defined by Law

[1138] As a police force, the Carabinieri are functionally dependent on the Minister of the Interior and carry out judicial police and public order and security tasks

[1139] Military Tasks The military tasks of the Carabinieri are: • contributing to the defense of the homeland and the protection of free institutions and the welfare of the national community in cases of public disaster in accordance with art. 1 of Law 382/78; • participating in peacekeeping operations outside the national territory

[1140] • participation in military police operations abroad and, on the basis of international agreements and mandates, contribution to the reconstruction of local police forces in the areas where the Armed Forces are present

[1141] in peace support missions; • exclusive exercise of military police and security functions for the Army, the Navy and the Air Force, as well as, pursuant to the Military Penal Codes, exercise of Military Judicial Police functions under the Military Justice bodies; • security of Italian diplomatic and consular representations, including that of military attachés abroad

[1142] • assistance to commands and military units engaged in institutional activities in the national territory, contribution to the mobilization service

[1182] The definition of “missions”

[1183] Introduction When the restructuring had already reached an advanced stage of implementation, precisely at the beginning of 1999, the Minister of Defence pro-tempore issued the first "ministerial directive" drawn up by the Defence General Staff and submitted to it for approval

[1184] For the record, it is worth mentioning the intention to align the “ministerial directive” with the “Ministerial Guidance” that the Alliance's Defence Ministers approve every two years and which represents the political directive for the subsequent planning activities of NATO's Military Authorities in the medium term

[1185] In particular, the Minister of Defence pro-tempore, in December 1998, in Brussels, had approved, together with his colleagues from the Alliance, the “NATO Ministerial Guidance 1998” which recommended the need to resolve the military deficiencies of the forces assigned to NATO in the following sectors: • intelligence and surveillance

[1186] • command and control; • deployability of forces (strategic transport, autonomy and logistical sustainability); • active and passive measures and deterrent capacity against the risk and threat of weapons of mass destruction (WMD); • increasing interoperability and cooperation capabilities between NATO forces and partner countries; • maintaining adequate military budget levels

[1187] In summary, the "Ministerial Directive 1999" was intended to constitute the first national attempt to set the Armed Forces' subsequent planning activities on the authoritative basis of upstream directives issued by the Minister

[1188] The "Directive" was supposed to be updated every two years, that is, in January 2001. From the "directive" was supposed to emanate, under the care of the Chief of Defence Staff, an implementing document, called the "strategic concept", which was issued on 28 December

[1189] Therefore, the “ministerial directive” and the “strategic concept”, issued after the restructuring brought about by the various Legislative Decrees, could not constitute the logical basis for the formation of the new Italian defensive instrument

[1190] They therefore translated into indications for the use of the instrument and as ideas for improvements to be made to the structure during construction

[1191] Hence the definition of "missions," to be understood as the translation of legislative norms into the national and international framework and therefore the implementation of the directives of national security policy

[1192] The Missions These are, therefore, missions which, without prejudice to the tasks of the Armed Forces established by Law 331/2000, may be subject to variations in accordance with the changing global strategic scenario

[1193] First mission: Defense of the country's vital interests against any possible aggression, in order to safeguard

[1194] • the integrity of the national territory understood as land platform, airspace and territorial waters

[1195] • the safety and freedom of communication routes

[1196] • the security of areas of national sovereignty and of compatriots abroad

[1197] It derives directly from the constitutional provision and was developed through the reunification of the pre-existing Armed Forces missions relating to the defense of the national territory

[1198] It should be emphasized that the reference to the integrity of the national territory and the security and freedom of communication routes does not limit the defense of the country's vital interests to traditional forms of threat alone, but can be extended to more recent forms of asymmetric conflict, such as defense against terrorist attacks or the use of weapons of mass destruction

[1199] Second mission: Safeguarding Euro-Atlantic spaces, within the framework of the country's strategic and/or vital interests, through contributing to NATO's collective defense

[1200] This mission is based on the agreements signed and ratified by Parliament relating to NATO and in the statements of the new Strategic Concept of the Atlantic Alliance, signed in Washington in the Third Mission Management of International Crises

[1201] Participation in crisis prevention and management operations, aimed at ensuring peace, security, stability, and international law, as well as the affirmation of fundamental human rights, in the spirit of the United Nations Charter, within international organizations and/or bi-multilateral agreements, with particular regard to Europe's autonomous crisis management capacity

[1202] The third mission arises from a specific political will, consistently confirmed over the last twenty years and formalized, in fact, with the Ministerial Directive of 1999 which led the Armed Forces to participate in crisis prevention and management actions approved by the UN, or in any case inspired by the principles set forth in the United Nations Charter, according to three possible intervention modes: • in the role of "Lead Nation" (for example, Operation "ALBA"); • as a Force forming part of a Coalition (such as NATO, the EU and the WEU

[1203] • following bi-multilateral agreements (Technical-Military Mission to Malta

[1204] Contribution to the protection of free institutions and performance of specific tasks in circumstances of public calamity and in other cases of extraordinary necessity and urgency

[1205] Directly borrowed from the law, reiterated in the legislation on professionals (Law 14 November 2000, n. 331 previously cited

[1206] The four missions require a remarkable set of skills to complete

[1207] The first two missions, by their nature, constitute the most demanding commitments and the available capabilities allow for the spectrum of expected needs to be met

[1208] These same capabilities are also required for the broad range of operations included in the third mission

[1209] Since this is characterized by an extreme variability of operational situations, it is necessary that the capabilities are scalable in the application of military force

[1210] With respect to the fourth mission, it should be underlined that the Armed Forces

[1211] They will not have to acquire specific skills, as those already possessed will be used, in compliance with the specificities of the job

[1212] Finally, to conclude the review of the tasks that the Armed Forces

[1213] they should perform, it is worth remembering the so-called external functions, that is, those not directly connected to the performance of the institutional tasks of the Defense

[1214] These are needs regulated by laws or decrees, characterised by undoubted public utility and in which the Armed Forces

[1215] provide, "compatibly with the technical capabilities of the staff and the resources available, their contribution in the fields of public utility and environmental protection" (Legislative Decree

[1216] n. 464/97, art

[1217] Among the main of these external functions are: assistance in the water supply of the smaller islands territorially incorporated into the regions with special statutes, when the conditions of particular need arise as foreseen by the specific program agreements defined with the Regions involved (MM); state civil air transport (AMI); air transport for the relief of the seriously ill and injured (EI, MMI, AMI, CC); relief and assistance in the event of natural disasters

[1218] • fire-fighting intervention

[1219] The capabilities considered fundamental, also on the basis of the commitments made to meet the Headline Goal (20 November 2000), are: timely availability of forces, interoperability, ability to operate in multinational contexts, deployment and mobility, C4ISR, precision and lethality of engagement, logistical sustainability, survivability and force protection

[1220] • the deactivation of unexploded ordnance

[1221] • the hydrographic service

[1222] • the lighthouse and maritime signalling service

[1223] • the adaptation of services for civil air traffic at military airports open to civil traffic and radio assistance at smaller airports

[1224] • contributions to the Italian Red Cross for the functioning of the Auxiliary Military Corps of the Armed Forces and the Volunteer Nurses Corps

[1225] International Crisis Management As part of the activities envisaged by the 3rd mission, Italy has pursued an intense cooperation policy aimed at promoting regional stability

[1226] In fact, Italy is the third country in the world, after the USA and the United Kingdom, for overall contribution to military peacekeeping operations, including participation in missions directly managed by the UN and presence in multinational operations under UN mandate

[1227] The missions in which our forces have taken or are taking part are essentially of four types: • peacekeeping in the classical sense

[1228] • police missions in support of peace-making or stabilization operations

[1229] • stabilization missions following peacekeeping operations

[1230] • international assistance missions

[1231] Italy's contribution to peacekeeping missions under the auspices of the United Nations has always been significant

[1232] Already in the first half of the 1990s, Italy was the second largest troop contributor to all operations under UN mandate, and its financial contribution to the ordinary budget is the fifth largest, in addition to that dedicated to the 17 current missions directly managed by the UN

[1325] Beyond the quantitative aspects, this offer is mainly qualified by the provision of three framework commands at Brigade/Regiment level, one of which is rapidly deployable, which will provide the backbone on which to insert the modular contributions offered by other Member States

[1326] The European Union Integrated Police Units will therefore be capable of rapid deployment, flexible and interoperable with the military component, logistical autonomy, and expressly inspired by the experience gained with the MSU

[1327] Publications Peace Studies Centre www.studiperlapace.it ____________ PART III THE ECONOMY 3.1 BREAKDOWN OF DEFENSE EXPENDITURE 3.2 BUDGET FORMATION 3.3 HISTORICAL SERIES 3.4 COSTS 3.5 CONCLUSIONS/CONSIDERATIONS 3.1 Breakdown of Defense Expenditure The financial resources allocated to Defense are divided according to their destination into: - expenses for the Defense Function relating to the fulfillment of the purely institutional tasks devolved to the three Armed Forces (Army, Navy and Air Force); - expenses for the Public Security Function allocated to meet the needs of the Carabinieri; - expenses for External Functions devolved to meet particular needs, regulated by Laws or Decrees, which are not directly connected with the institutional tasks of Defense

[1328] expenses for Provisional Pensions relating to the payment of provisional retirement benefits to military personnel in the auxiliary position (period following cessation of active service during which the military personnel may be retained or recalled to service

[1329] In order to proceed with the technical-financial processing, these expenses are further broken down into expenses linked to "laws" and those linked to "programs

[1330] Expenses tied to "laws" are those that are mandatory in nature as they are determined, including their amount, by provisions of law and/or government resolutions

[1331] These charges are subject to automatic mechanisms that make them particularly stringent precisely because they are linked to laws and/or inter-ministerial or international agreements

[1332] These may also include specific needs related to public utility services such as, for example, water supply to smaller islands, activities in support of civil aviation, state civil air transport, and assistance for the seriously ill and injured

[1333] Expenditure tied to "programs" is intended to ensure the functionality, efficiency and effectiveness of the military instrument and arises from the programmatic choices identified by the General Staffs, the General Secretariat of Defence and the General Command of the Carabinieri (called the Armed Forces and Joint Planning Bodies – OP) and approved by the Chief of Defence Staff

[1334] Subsequently, for the preparation of the budget, expenditures are divided into three distinct "sectors": personnel, relating to the costs to be borne for the salaries and allowances of permanent military personnel, civilian personnel with continuous employment, the economic treatment of conscripts, and the temporary retirement benefits of military personnel; operations, relating to the costs necessary to ensure the functionality and efficiency of the military instrument (expenses for education and training, for the maintenance and support of vehicles, materials, and infrastructure, for the operation of Commands/Institutions/Departments); investments, relating to the costs necessary to improve the effectiveness of the military instrument (expenses for the modernization and renewal of operational vehicles, for technical-logistical support and infrastructure, and for research and development

[1335] The first two sectors (personnel and operations) determine the costs related to the "operation" of the Armed Forces, while the last concerns the acquisition of durable goods, which in turn promote security and technological progress. Budget Formation Spending forecasts are prepared based on the objectives and indications provided by: - the Government, with the Economic and Financial Planning Document (DPEF); - the Minister of Economy and Finance, with the annual circular on budget forecasts

[1336] Minister of Defense, with regard to the financial hypothesis to be used as a reference (percentage ratio to be ensured between Defense Budget/GDP and Defense Function/GDP) and with the Investment Planning Document

[1337] Chief of the Defence Staff, with the “Directive for the preparation of the budget estimate”

[1338] They are prepared by the Central Office of Budget and Financial Affairs (BILANDIFE) and by the Defence General Staff on the basis of the proposals and data processed by the OPs and then submitted for approval to the Chief of Defence who, after consulting the Committee of Chiefs of Staff, sends the project to the Minister for examination for approval

[1339] BILANDIFE then proceeds to draft the technical financial budget and, after approval by the Minister, following the opinion of the Supreme Council of the Armed Forces, transmits it to the State General Accounting Office for its relevant assessments and subsequent presentation to the government and parliament (Budget Bill

[1340] Before the parliamentary debate on financial measures (Budget Bills, Finance Bills, and related provisions) begins, the Defence General Staff prepares and transmits to the Minister's Cabinet, for the Minister's approval and subsequent forwarding to the parliamentary committees, the "Additional Note to the Defence Budget." Through this document, the Minister of Defence outlines to Parliament the goals and objectives that his Ministry intends to pursue

[1341] Following the approval of the Budget Law, the "Budget Estimates for the financial year" are drawn up

[1350] They constitute a tool with extremely high technological content and, consequently, high cost due to the inherent need to always maintain a competitive advantage at the highest levels

[1351] This has an initial impact, obviously, on the resources that must be constantly and adequately allocated to Investment and Strengthening

[1352] But immediately after the completion of each planned project, the Armed Forces must absorb operating costs that, precisely because of their high technological content, are generally quite considerable. Indeed, the entry into service of a new weapons system is associated with the need to build and/or adapt infrastructure, initiate training programs and dedicated exercises, and maintain the system itself in terms of numbers and efficiency, in addition to numerous other activities that indirectly contribute to general support or that in any case constitute costs that are passed on to the individual company

[1353] The costs of the various military components of each Af (for example the brigade, the ship, the wing) arise from statistical processing based on information acquired through automated detection systems which, depending on the component under examination, have as their object of investigation

[1354] its actual strength

[1355] training activities (exercises and courses) and operations conducted on national territory in the year under review; - the infrastructure used and the consumption associated with their use

[1356] the equipment and materials and related consumption

[1357] These systems represent a highly valuable tool both for carrying out the necessary cost-effectiveness checks - in the financial planning/programming phase, as well as in the organizational-executive phase of the annual budget - and for estimating

[1358] any costs incurred for the creation of a new component of a different type (set-up costs); - the possible savings that can be achieved in the event of the dissolution or change in type of a component

[1359] the levels of efficiency and effectiveness of the component, through comparisons between the reference standard costs and those actually incurred

[1360] Standard costs represent the “optimal” costs that each facility should approach to ensure maximum cost-effectiveness

[1361] They are drawn up taking into account financial data relating to seven typologies or macroaggregates

[1362] fixed costs (including salaries, wages and expenses for food, clothing and hygiene) for infrastructure, training, healthcare, maintenance of efficiency, maintenance of personnel and residual costs

[1363] It should be emphasized, however, that costs are significantly affected by any changes that may occur in the FA's architecture, in the structure of the individual components, or in the tasks and functions they develop

[1364] Furthermore, a further factor affecting their variability is represented by "military inflation" - very different from the more well-known national inflation - which must be resorted to given the particular characteristics of military spending which, due to its atypical nature, is ill-suited to the use of classic national-level indicators (Gross Domestic Product, general government indices, etc

[1365] By way of example, the following are indicated in

[1366] Table 7, the expenses necessary for the operation, or for the maintenance and carrying out of institutional training and operational activities, of some typical components of the three Armed Forces; - Table 8, the acquisition costs of some significant vehicles and units; - Table 9, the costs per flight hour of Air Force aircraft from which it is clear that one hour of flight for a TORNADO, excluding depreciation costs, costs over 18,000 euros (approximately 35 million); - Table 10, the daily costs for the use of naval units and vehicles; - Table 11, costs per flight hour of Navy aircraft

[1367] In this context, it is important to highlight that the resources that the Ministry of Defense allocates to the operation of the military instrument should not be considered pure "management costs" but, in a much stricter sense, true tools of functionality and efficiency

[1368] And all this is particularly true in the current delicate transition phase towards a professional model, where the quality of personnel training is accompanied by the availability of an aging fleet of materials, vehicles, and facilities, requiring constant and increasingly costly maintenance and repairs

[1373] Conclusions/Considerations: The recovery of the state budget and public finances is destined to profoundly change the way the economy functions, generating new resources for investments that benefit the community

[1374] For its part, the Ministry of Defense has overcome a historic obstacle in budget preparation with the creation of a single Head of the Armed Forces and has increased spending effectiveness with the restructuring of central and peripheral agencies and a significant downsizing of operational units

[1375] The effects of this constant effort have materialized over the past two years with encouraging growth figures for both operating and investment expenses, which in 2001 recorded increases of 3% and 8% respectively compared to the previous year

[1376] However, these data should not obscure the fact that Italy, among the European countries most homogeneous in size and with GDP values in the same order of magnitude as the national average, has the lowest defense spending in absolute terms, both per capita and in terms of its impact on their respective GDPs

[1377] In fact, for the Defence Function Italy spends a sum equal to approximately 47% of that sustained by France and 32% of that sustained by the United Kingdom, as can be seen from the graph in Table

[1378] Similarly, with reference to the impact on GDP, Italian spending is just over half that of France and 40% of that of the United Kingdom (Graph Table 13), while, comparing per capita spending for the Defense Function (Graph Table 14), we find that in 2001, compared to Italy's 218 € (approximately 422 thousand lire), the French invested 423 € (820 thousand) and the British dedicated 642 € (1 million and 245 thousand). It is in this mandatory scenario of integration with the corresponding instruments of European partners that Defense must develop and propose new financial hypotheses, taking into account the multiple gaps that make consequent political action difficult to avoid

[1379] Parliament, through the approval of recent appropriations, has demonstrated that a new consensus is emerging on the need for a measured, effective spending increase that responds to Italy's real strategic needs

[1380] It is therefore to be expected that, following the current contingent situation, characterised by a process of recovering the financial shortfalls of previous years, the resources allocated to Defence should be more significant starting in

[1381] The decision of European countries to accelerate the process of developing their own autonomous military intervention capacity and the commitment to establish a European Rapid Response Force by 2003, together with the recent parliamentary recognition of the “professionalization” of the military instrument, constitute the cardinal factors on which to base any financial estimate

[1382] To this end, it seems reasonable to hypothesize a gradual increase in the Defense Budget/GDP ratio from the current 1.5% to approximately 2% in the medium term. This, if the country's positive economic trend is confirmed, would allow for the provision of adequate resources and programmatic certainty for a military instrument capable of operating with an adequate level of efficiency and effectiveness and of competing, with a view to complete interoperability, with that of other allied nations

[1383] In this case, the priority allocation of resources should be directed both towards the growing operating costs associated with an increasingly sophisticated instrument, both qualitatively and technologically, which requires training cycles different from those currently in place, and towards the essential modernization and adaptation programs capable of filling the technological gap within the timeframe required by the international commitments undertaken, reversing the historical trend of undercapitalization

[1384] In a second phase, the operational components will be renewed, prioritizing the modernization of the operational lines and older vehicles

[1385] In this latter context, the use of special laws to finance one or more major programs—an instrument that in the past has allowed the Armed Forces to undertake several major programs, thus enabling the modernization of the military—seems the most appropriate solution to ensure the short to medium-term financial certainty needed to initiate a renewal process consistent with the timeline dictated by pressing, and now no longer postponable, needs

[1386] To this end, an extraordinary legislative provision is being prepared which should financially support, through a spending forecast of 7.5 million euros (approximately 14,500 billion), to be implemented over a ten-year period, those priority programs which can be completed in a relatively short time frame and at pre-established costs

[1393] Tasks-Organization The organization of the Defence as regards the industrial apparatus, is headed by the administrative area headed by the Secretary General/DNA, on whom the 10 General Directorates of the Ministry depend

[1394] In his capacity as DNA (National Armaments Director), the Secretary General is responsible for directing research, development, and acquisition activities for weapons systems, based on the programs defined by the Chief of Defence Staff

[1395] In this context, it participates in high international forums in the framework of the implementation of multinational agreements

[1396] The SG/DNA is a member of the Supreme Council of the Armed Forces, the Chiefs of Staff Committee, and is Chairman of the Advisory Committee that reviews major armaments contracts

[1397] He is also Vice President of the Defense - Industry Committee, chaired by the Minister of Defense

[1409] The Defence Industry Sector 4.3.1 Organizational Structure - Pre-Reform The entities of the Technical-Industrial Area of Defence (35 Establishments and Arsenals) pre-reform (law 28 December 1995, n. 549) constituted a legacy that Defence had been carrying with it since the First World War

[1410] At the time, they represented production entities which, over the years, essentially became maintenance entities

[1411] Of these, 24 were from the Army, 9 from the Navy while 3 had a distinctly joint character

[1412] The Air Force has never had any factories or arsenals as it has always relied on the civilian companies and enterprises that produce the aircraft for production and for 4th level maintenance

[1413] The main provisions to which the pre-existing Technical-Industrial Area of Defense referred are to be found in Presidential Decree no. 1481 of 18 November 1965, Presidential Decree no. 1077 of 5 June 1976, and Ministerial Decree no. 23 December

[1414] In particular: with the Presidential Decree 1481 the basic rules for the reorganisation and modernisation of military establishments and arsenals were defined, as production and work bodies, placed under the control of the General Directorates

[1415] • Presidential Decree no. 1077 of 5 June 1976 constituted the implementing regulation for the functioning of industrial military establishments and arsenals

[1416] It identified the categories of establishments classified as

[1417] large, medium and small potential

[1418] Furthermore, all the competences to which the aforementioned institutions had to respond were specified in detail
